Claude's reply:
I checked all ten transcripts and NASA's project page. The findings are in `sources_check.md`, the only file I wrote. The PDFs are in a temporary folder outside the project.

**All ten URLs work.** Each one opened as a PDF, and every name and date matches the transcript's title block and opening lines. Each transcript also ends with "[End of interview]", so the downloads are complete.

**Roles:**
- **Royce Mitchell: wrong in your table.** He wasn't the External Tank manager. On p. 3 he says he was sent after Challenger "to join the solid rocket motor project as manager of solid rocket motor." NASA's page lists him as "Reusable Solid Rocket Motor Project Manager."
- **Gerald Smith: understated.** Most of his career was on the Space Shuttle main engine. After Challenger he worked on the booster redesign, then "took over the SRB Project from Larry Mulloy" (pp. 26–27). That makes him the Solid Rocket Booster project manager, not just a redesign engineer.
- **Thomas Moser:** the role is right. But the transcript header says "NASA Johnson Space Center Oral History Project," not STS Recordation, though NASA's STS page lists him anyway. There's also a second session (5/27/2010, `mosertl-5-27-10.pdf`) that's missing from your table.
- **Terrence White and Gerald Blackburn:** their titles appear only on NASA's page. White's transcript shows a technician who became a heat-shield tile (thermal protection system) supervisor; it never says "project lead." Blackburn worked for the contractor Rockwell and led a Materials Control and Specifications group of about 30 people.
- **Thomas, Singer, Pessin, Odom, Sheehan:** the transcripts confirm the roles in your table.

**How the interviews were made:**
- **Who conducted them:** NASA historians Rebecca Wright and Jennifer Ross-Nazzal, as named in each title block and opening paragraph.
- **Recording:** NASA's page says the transcripts "are created from audio-recorded oral history interviews." Blackburn's session was also videotaped by a third party (p. 1).
- **Verbatim or edited: edited.** Every PDF's header reads "EDITED ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPT." NASA's page says they are "presented with limited revisions," with brackets and ellipses marking edits. Mitchell's transcript alone has about 188 bracketed insertions. The page doesn't say whether the interviewees reviewed their transcripts.

**This affects two things in notes.md:**
1. The line "each transcript is a verbatim record" is false. Quotes should be presented as coming from edited transcripts, with bracketed text marked as the editors'.
2. The draft methods paragraph ("We conducted ten semi-structured interviews… recorded and transcribed them") is false. This is secondary analysis of archival interviews done by NASA historians in 2010–2011.

The page numbers in the file are exact where I quote the first few pages. Those marked "p. ~" are my estimates from where the passage falls in the extracted text, so check them before citing.

Outside this task, a few things in notes.md look wrong too:
- Vaughan (1996) argued against the "amoral calculation" explanation, not for it.
- Columbia was hit by foam insulation from the External Tank, not ice.
- Edmondson's psychological safety article is 1999, not 2001.
- Gioia's method starts with first-order concepts from the informants' own words, not with dimensions taken from the literature.

I can fix these when we move on.

## How the interviews were made

- **Who conducted them:** NASA JSC History Office historians, not us. Rebecca
  Wright and Jennifer Ross-Nazzal ran them (Sandra Johnson assisted on Moser),

- **Verbatim or edited:** **Edited.** Every PDF's header says "EDITED ORAL
  HISTORY TRANSCRIPT." NASA page: "presented with limited revisions … Brackets
  and ellipses indicate where the text has been annotated or edited for
  clarity." Brackets are common (e.g. 188 bracketed insertions in Mitchell, 131
  in Moser). The page doesn't say whether interviewees reviewed their transcripts.
- **Project scope:** interview dates on the NASA page run from 4/9/2010 to
  4/15/2012. "Titles listed reflect the positions that the subject held while
  involved with the program."

## Implications for notes.md

- "Each transcript is a verbatim record" is false. Quotes are from edited
  transcripts. Bracketed text belongs to the editors and should be marked as such.
- The draft methods paragraph ("We conducted ten semi-structured interviews …
  recorded and transcribed them") is false. This is secondary analysis of
  archival oral histories conducted by NASA historians in 2010–2011.
- Table fixes: Mitchell's role (RSRM, not ET); Smith (SRB project manager after

Claude's reply:
The eleven transcripts are now in `transcripts/`: ten PDFs plus Moser's 5/27/2010 session, each with a `.txt` version. The `.txt` files have one form-feed page break per PDF page, so the page numbers below match the PDF footers.

Six parallel readers each read one or two transcripts in full. I then checked about 35 of their quoted phrases against the text, and all but one were on the pages they reported. That one was Mitchell's "simplest elements" quote, which is on p. 30, not p. 31; it's corrected below. The "N of M pages" figures are the readers' estimates. I also fixed one citation in my own `sources_check.md`: Mitchell's "manager of solid rocket motor" quote is on p. 4, not p. 3.

**Royce Mitchell** (NASA Marshall; engineer, then manager; 46 pp.) – Almost entirely about Challenger. He was project manager for the redesigned solid rocket motor from 1986 to about 1990, chosen partly because he "was not on the project at the time of the accident" (p. 5). Columbia gets one remark on p. 30: "the two simplest elements … killed the two crews." About 15–18 pages concern settling technical disputes as a manager:
- p. 9: two competing redesign teams.
- pp. 17–18, 24: clashes with the National Research Council oversight panel over the deliberately flawed test motor.
- pp. 20–26: the outer boot ring change he "let [him]self get talked into," which failed in test and led to "a more painful day" before Truly (p. 26).
- pp. 36–37: formal design reviews.
- pp. 38–39: the debate over cork debris.
- pp. 30–31: a Thiokol worker secretly tamping down putty blowholes in test motors ("almost criminal"). This whole passage is in editorial brackets, so it was probably added when Mitchell reviewed the transcript, not spoken in the interview.

**John W. Thomas** (NASA engineer and manager until 1989, then Lockheed; 29 pp.) – Challenger only; Columbia never appears. He "essentially ran the Accident Analysis Panel" (pp. 2–5), then led the solid rocket motor redesign team (pp. 5–29). About 10–12 pages are the team leader settling technical questions, not raising concerns from below:
- p. 9: "we moved on as I had the final vote."
- pp. 10–12: tests to settle open hypotheses.
- pp. 8, 14–18: outside oversight, including heaters the panel insisted on that his team thought unnecessary.
- p. 20: Kennedy inspections he found "overzealous."

It reads as a tidy success story with little dissent.

**Gerald W. Smith** (NASA Marshall; engineer, then manager; 52 pp.) – Mainly Challenger. He was in Washington as NASA Headquarters' main engine expert when it happened (p. 26), then became Solid Rocket Booster project manager after Mulloy (pp. 27–43). On pp. 49–50 he says Marshall candidates "had been implicated by … the telecon the night before." Columbia gets one passage on debris "finger pointing" (p. 35). This is one of the richest transcripts, with about 15–17 pages of specific episodes:
- p. 2: as a young engineer, told no when he asked to change the tile.
- pp. 17–19: changing charts "in ways I didn't even like" after an internal review.
- pp. 22–23: pushed by Lindstrom past Engineering's official position to give his own opinion, which upset his boss.
- pp. 31–32: "I lost the argument" over the flawed-motor tests.
- pp. 32–34: after Challenger, an engineering staff that was "very risk-averse" and wrote 6,000–7,000 review discrepancies.
- pp. 37–38: friction with the new independent Quality office.
- p. 41: an all-night debate over a heater short before he said "go ahead and wake the crew."

**Jody A. Singer** (NASA Marshall; manager throughout, no engineering work described; 20 pp.) – Columbia is the focus. Her first launch as reusable solid rocket motor project manager was STS-107 (p. 3), and pp. 8–16 cover return to flight. Challenger is only career context (p. 1). About 9–10 pages concern concerns, but they are general and procedural rather than episodes:
- "Did we make it safe enough?" (pp. 8–10).
- Return to flight gave people leeway to ask "Why?" (pp. 13–14).
- "I believe you, but demonstrate it" (p. 15).
- Launch-readiness polling and the mission management team (pp. 17–19).

The bolt-catcher story (pp. 11–12) is secondhand. Her dates conflict: RSRM manager "2002 until 2005" (p. 3) vs. "2002 to 2007" (p. 8).

**Myron "Mike" Pessin** (Chrysler contractor briefly, then NASA Marshall; engineer, then External Tank chief engineer from 1988; 60 pp.) – Both accidents, but mostly tank design and manufacturing history. Challenger, pp. 44–47: the tank as "a victim … not the aggressor." Afterward, every repair record was reviewed and crack decisions were taken from floor quality supervisors and given to engineering. Columbia, pp. 27–29, is the key passage for your question:
- Foam loss "was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety."
- The tank project's deputy tried to open an in-flight anomaly two flights before the accident and was told "we know about foam coming off."
- The bipod fix was then handled as a routine change.

He had retired by then and declines to discuss the investigation (pp. 55–56). About 8–10 pages are directly relevant; smaller episodes are on pp. 18–23, 34–37, 45 and 49–52.

**James B. Odom** (NASA Marshall; External Tank project manager for 11 years, later director of engineering; 30 pp.) – Barely touches either accident. Columbia is never mentioned. On Challenger he says only that he was "enjoined" from working on it (p. 22). The ice and foam requirement on pp. 8–9 and 17 is not linked to an accident. Only about 2–3 pages concern concerns, and those are design and test lessons (pp. 16–17, 20, 25). It is the weakest fit for your question.

**Gerald D. Sheehan** (contractor: North American, then Rockwell, then Boeing; engineer, Columbia's vehicle manager from about 1978, manager from the mid-1990s; 43 pp.) – Challenger never appears. Columbia the accident gets one line (p. 41); elsewhere "Columbia" means the vehicle being prepared for STS-1. Still, it has about 12–14 strong pages:
- pp. 5–12: his year-and-a-half fight to make Marshall and Martin prevent tank ice that could strike the orbiter. It ended with roughly 1,300 lb of added foam and "I was never welcome in Marshall after that" (p. 9). This is useful background to the foam-debris story.
- p. 26: "wink-wink, nod-nod" on the 160-hour turnaround.
- pp. 27–33: pitching changes to NASA as vehicle manager, including arguing against a retrofit (pp. 31–32).

The transcript doesn't say whether he was still vehicle manager in 1986.

**Terrence R. White** (technician, then thermal protection system supervisor; employer never stated, apparently a Kennedy processing contractor, not NASA; 52 pp.) – Both accidents, told from the shop floor.
- Columbia: the new gap-filler fix and tighter repair criteria for return to flight (pp. 9–10, 18–20), and investigation test panels (p. 35).
- Challenger: the Rogers Commission found "the shop folks had too much control," so responsibility moved to engineers (pp. 32–33), and repair paperwork grew from three pages to 21 (pp. 48–49).

About 8–10 pages concern concerns, e.g. "it took a while to convince the program" (p. 8) and his challenge to a cure time (p. 39). "Project lead" appears nowhere. This is the only voice from the technician level.

**Thomas L. Moser, two sessions** (NASA Johnson; engineer, then structural design head, deputy Orbiter project manager and director of engineering; 48 + 25 pp.; both headed "Johnson Space Center Oral History Project") – The material on concerns is mostly about the pre-STS-1 tile crisis.
- Session 1: margin decisions criticized as "crazy as hell" (p. 23), and the core tile pages, including "Get the son of a bitch in space" (pp. 37–44). About 12 of 48 pages.
- Session 2: "Us grunt engineers were trying to say, 'We think we need more tests'" (p. 3), and the escalation with Yardley, Kraft and Houbolt the day before launch (pp. 6–9). About 9 of 25 pages.
- Challenger: both sessions say he led an internal NASA investigation in the first days (s1 p. 48; s2 pp. 21–23). Neither mentions a board or commission.
- Columbia: only session 2, pp. 10–11, where he relays secondhand that there was "some push to say that debris impact was okay."

**Gerald Blackburn** (contractor: Rockwell, later a Boeing consultant after Columbia; materials engineer, then manager of a 30-person group from about 1980; 44 pp.) – Both accidents, briefly.

but needed to eliminate ice. That was the big driver. So we covered the LOX [liquid oxygen]

forward attach, which is a bipod spindle, has to move. Then as you fly and you start putting

so we were going to have to underlay it with ablator. You put the ablator underneath because if

you put it on top, the foam would sublime out from underneath the ablator and the ablator would

30 June 2010                                                                                    16

critical it is so we’re going to have to go back and test it.” The test series meant going into the

=== PDF page 10 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

THOMAS: It was actually very positive; there was no hostility or being protective, resentful, or
anything of that nature one might expect under those circumstances. Their sole interest was
initially finding the cause of the accident, finding the remedies to prevent it from happening in
the future, and regaining their pride in producing the quality Shuttle motors. They were very
positive, very cooperative, and we evolved into a good cohesive team.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Would you tell us about the testing program once you had come up with this
design and how you wanted to test it? Would you talk about the different tests that you
conducted on the motors?

THOMAS: We had some very unique test facilities that were constructed specifically for
developing and testing the redesigned motor at both subscale and full-scale test articles. We
developed and constructed a field joint test article facility that consisted of two inert full-scale
half-motor segments with a forward dome, aft dome, and a nozzle simulator. We could place
differing amounts of propellant inside test article and simulate the joint performance as the
pressure increased at motor ignition on the launch pad.
    We constructed another similar facility in the MSFC Test Division where the former
Apollo J-2 engine test stand was converted into a motor test facility where we could apply the
external loads associated with structural members that attach the motors to the external tank.
This facility was brought online because there was some speculation that there were unusual
loads induced into the motor aft field joint by these attach struts causing the joint to open and

29 June 2010 10

=== PDF page 11 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

leak. We had to produce a test that could prove this hypothesis to be either positive or negative;
and it turned out to be negative as we always thought.
    We also constructed a test facility for the case-to-nozzle joint which was redesigned. It
served the same purpose for the case nozzle joint as the field joint test facility did for the case
field joint. Additionally, we tested small test motors, 48-inch vice, 12 foot in diameter at MSFC,
as well as many smaller motors at Thiokol, to explore different concepts and to verify our
analysis tools. Finally we had three full-scale motors; DM-8 and 9 [development motor] and
QM-6 [qualification motor] that were tested in Utah. A second full scale motor test stand was
constructed at Thiokol to test the motors as rapidly as possible and to modernize the stand data
acquisition system.
    The existing facility was designated T-24, and the new one was T-97. Everything
redesigned and everything that was questioned prior to design had a test fixture or test stand to
prove or disprove the hypothesis, or to demonstrate that the design was successful. For example,
prior to Challenger, the motor had never been tested at low temperature, so we covered the test
stand, installed a conditioning system, and brought the temperature down in the range of 40
degrees. The cover was then quickly removed and the motor was fired right away. We
demonstrated that it would operate properly at the lower temperatures.
    We also performed some unique testing that had not been done previously on large solid
rocket motors and those involved intentionally flawing the joint seals and sealing surfaces in the
redesigned joints. We began by inducing flaws the insulation, then the first O-ring, and followed
with the secondary O-ring. All these tests were successful, and thus demonstrated that the motor
would perform satisfactorily even if flaws found their way into the joints.

29 June 2010 11

=== PDF page 12 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

ROSS-NAZZAL: What did people think when you suggested that idea to perform a test with
flaws?

THOMAS: When intentionally flawing the motor first came up, I was among those that said,
“You mean what?” But the more we thought about it, and the more confidence that we gained in
our design, we thought it to be a good idea.

ROSS-NAZZAL: And it proved that the SRM was safe?

THOMAS: Right, completely safe. The only unusual observation to date was a small amount of
combustion gas by-products, soot, penetrated the insulation J-Seal. They attributed the small
blow-by to a change in the adhesive by the vendor. Many were upset about it, but it actually was
of no consequence whatsoever. We in fact discussed the need for that adhesive after we got into
testing; I didn’t think it was necessary but we kept it as a redundant way of keeping the
insulation joint mating surfaces closed.

ROSS-NAZZAL: I’ve been reading the book Truth, Lies and O-Rings [:Inside the Space Shuttle
Challenger Disaster], and Al [Allan J.] McDonald talks about after some of the tests how you
and he or Royce [E.] Mitchell would actually physically go into the SRM to check things out.
Would you tell us about your recollections of that?

THOMAS: Yes, we entered the motors for pretest inspections and after every flight configured
motor test; we did the same in the field joint test article motors. The full motors were tested

29 June 2010 12

=== PDF page 14 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

ROSS-NAZZAL: How were you able to achieve so much so quickly, in such a short amount of
time, in terms of testing and then requalifying the SRB for flight in a period of less than three
years?

THOMAS: We were working quite intensely; many hours a day, six and seven days a week. We
had a talented, dedicated team with focused leadership who did not have to get permission from
many levels of management and organizations to implement designs, conduct tests, and perform
analyses. This process allowed us to move quite rapidly in that environment.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Did any changes have to be made to the design you had decided upon after any
of the tests that you conducted?

THOMAS: No changes were made in the joint areas after we baselined the configuration, but we
did have to tweak the design of a nozzle component following test DM-9. I understand that there
has been some refinements in the case nozzle and igniter joints in the years since returning to
flight.

ROSS-NAZZAL: That’s remarkable. Tell us about the media interest in the redesign effort out in
Utah.

THOMAS: The media was quite interested both at MSFC and in Utah. Our Marshall public
affairs organization was quite accommodating in releasing information and arranging for rather

29 June 2010 14

=== PDF page 15 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

frequent, periodic press conferences where I would inform the press on our progress, our
problems, how our design was evolving, and would respond to any questions they might have.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Had you had much experience working with the press before this event?

THOMAS: I had some experience in dealing with the media but had to come up very quickly on
the learning curve. When we were executing Spacelab and Skylab, I had some media interactive
training where specialists came in and suggested to us what to do, what not to do, and how to
behave. That training was very beneficial.

ROSS-NAZZAL: How did the [William P.] Rogers Commission [also known as the Presidential
Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident] affect the redesign effort, the analysis
and the eventual outcome of what you were working on at that point?

THOMAS: The Rogers Commission finished their work and released their report in June 1986,
which completed their task. They were therefore not around to influence the redesign, but
NASA stood up the National Research Council [NRC] panel comprised of recognized subject
matter experts that reported directly to the Administrator. They reviewed our work but did not
try to influence us one way or another on any particular design solution. Instead they would
come into either at MSFC or Utah for our team to brief them on our design solutions, analysis,
and test results.
    The only thing that they were really insistent upon was the joint heaters on the field joint
O-rings. Of course they had their thoughts about other design aspects and objectively reviewed

29 June 2010 15

=== PDF page 16 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

our solutions, analyses, and tests substantiating our decisions. I didn’t think the heaters were
necessary based on our tests, but it was a way of making the overall joint performance more
robust.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Was it challenging to include the heaters in the SRM?

THOMAS: Incorporating the joint heaters was a nuisance more than anything else. In fact the
Constellation Program has removed the heaters on the Ares I first stage, which is the same motor
but with one additional segment.
There was another oversight group that was established by the Marshall Center to review
our work, and that was an engineering group that was headed by Al [Allan] Norton, who was the
former external tank chief engineer. His team was composed of a number of engineering
managers including such recognized experts as Jim [James E.] Kingsbury from Marshall, Max
[Maxime A.] Faget from Houston [JSC], and Horace [L.] Lamberth from KSC.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Did you find that to be challenging with so many cooks in the kitchen so to
speak?

THOMAS: It distracted us a little bit, but it was probably productive.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Congress was also very interested in the redesign of the SRM. I think I saw that
you had testified. Would you tell us about their oversight and the interest that they had?

29 June 2010 16

=== PDF page 17 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

THOMAS: We were before congress and staff several times, giving them the results of our design
work and test results. They in fact produced a voluminous report of three or four volumes, based
on their staff work. We had staff members that would come occasionally to understand what we
were doing. We gave them the same type of information as that given the NRC panel and others.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Did they in any way influence the design or testing effort that you were working
under?

THOMAS: No, they were more interested in progress

ROSS-NAZZAL: What about the astronauts? I know that there were some astronauts who were
following the redesign effort.

THOMAS: The Astronaut Office assigned two crew members to participate with our team. The
senior astronaut was Hoot [Robert L.] Gibson and the other was Steve [Stephen S.] Oswald and
both stayed with us from the very start until we finished the design. There were others, like John
[W.] Young, who attended our major reviews. The dedicated members didn’t reside with us, but
they came as they felt necessary to participate in the design process, testing, test reviews, etc.

ROSS-NAZZAL: Were they pleased with the final design that you had come up with?

THOMAS: Yes, all were in agreement with design and test results.

29 June 2010 17

=== PDF page 18 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

ROSS-NAZZAL: Mr. Mitchell had mentioned the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel [ASAP] was
also very interested in following the redesign effort. Can you talk about their efforts?

THOMAS: We briefed the ASAP giving them the same type of information that we gave our
other oversight panels. I don’t recall them having any direct opposition to any of our design or
test plan or results.

ROSS-NAZZAL: It almost seems like there’s so many people overseeing the work that you were
doing that you may have spent more time handling these groups than maybe doing the redesign
and testing. Would that be an accurate assessment?

THOMAS: No, even though it took quite a bit of planning, logistics, and briefings, they were
actually quite supportive in their quest to be sure that we were considering all aspects that might
have influence or led to the accident.

ROSS-NAZZAL: When was the redesigned SRM finally qualified for flight?

THOMAS: The certification process begins with design and design reviews through development
and qualification testing to the flight readiness review, where certification of flight worthiness is
executed. We had qualification motor tests, other full and subscale testing, extensive analyses,
and manufacturing process records to support the certification for flightworthiness process. That
certification process culminated in the flight readiness review prior to STS-26 that flew
September of ’88.

29 June 2010 18

=== PDF page 20 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

THOMAS: There were S&MA [Safety and Mission Assurance] changes derived from re-
evaluating the failure mode and effects analysis and single point failures. This led us to
incorporate additional ports to leak-check both primary and secondary O-rings in the same
direction that they would be sealing during motor operation. Other changes related to the
amount of inspections including sealing surface smoothness inspections, dimensional
measurements on the two joint mating segments, and case roundness. We even had a “round
maker” tool that could return the case joints to a completely round condition before mating to
preclude unacceptable stresses.

ROSS-NAZZAL: You mentioned that you moved from Utah to Florida in preparation for the
return to flight effort. Would you tell us about going out to KSC and working on that effort?

THOMAS: I relocated to the Kennedy Space Center when the return to flight motors arrived there
as the Marshall representative to the KSC processing team. This was to expedite anything
requiring Marshall’s engineering disposition. At one point the processing team overzealous with
the number of measurements and inspections, like grease discoloration presence of human hair
and lint, etc. It got to the point where we were not making much progress, so the Center
Directors at KSC, Forrest [S.] McCartney, and Marshall, J. R. Thompson, agreed that they would
appoint me as the decision authority for processing SRBs in the VAB. As that became known, I
never had to exercise that authority. The team just turned to and got on with the job.

29 June 2010 20

=== PDF page 23 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

THOMAS: We had some pressure and thermal instrumentation, but most of the solid rocket
motors hardware performance information is obtained by inspecting the motors after they are
retrieved from the ocean and towed back into Hanger AF and disassembled after the flight..

ROSS-NAZZAL: Had the return to flight crew followed the redesign effort very closely, or were
they too busy?

THOMAS: They were mostly tied up in their training; but we talked to Fred [Frederick H.] Hauck
and Dick [Richard O.] Covey from time to time

ROSS-NAZZAL: I understand you remained at the Cape for the next flight of STS-27.

THOMAS: Yes, I stayed for the two flights and then returned to MSFC. I think it was on STS-27
that the Shuttle came back with a large number of damaged thermal protection tiles. I was asked
to form a team and determine the culprit. We determined that the damage was attributable to
insulation material shedding off the SRB nose cap during ascent and impacting the very fragile
tile. Following that assignment I retired from NASA in April of ’89 and joined Lockheed at
KSC launching Shuttles.

ROSS-NAZZAL: I wanted to ask you about the ASRM, when you started working for Lockheed.
Can you tell us what the advanced solid rocket motor was compared to the redesigned solid
rocket motor?

29 June 2010 23

=== PDF page 28 ===

STS Recordation Oral History Project John W. Thomas

ROSS-NAZZAL: I’m going to ask Rebecca if she has any questions for you.

WRIGHT: I just have one. You were talking about your design team in Utah and moving toward
final design and all the progress. Did you encounter setbacks where you thought maybe you
weren’t going to be able to encounter that progress?

THOMAS: We had some disappointments but they were mostly related to schedule; we were
trying to do things very rapidly to return to flight as soon as possible. But I don’t recall any great
hurdles that we ran into that just “it doesn’t look like we’re going to be able to pull this off.”
Early on, we took a motor of the Challenger configuration, attempted to trim away some of the
insulation at the joint, and incorporate a different insulation seal configuration. When we
finished manufacturing that design we looked at it and said, “We don’t want to do that, it’s not as
safe as we’d like to see, and for sure we don’t want to lose another motor.”

WRIGHT: Did you explore using different vendors and manufacturers, or did you stay with the
ones that had been chosen to do the original motor?

THOMAS: We stayed with the same suppliers because they were providing quality hardware and
were not at fault in the accident. It was also more expedient to remain with them from a
schedule perspective.

29 June 2010 28

MOSER: I had to feed my family, so probably really wouldn’t have done that. I started off in the
Shuttle Program when I was a subsystem manager for the Orbiter structure. I had the full
responsibility for all of the structural integrity of the Orbiter and then later became head of

head and my program responsibility for the development of the Shuttle—the Orbiter structure.
That was a challenge, a lot.
    The way we had it organized, when I was the head of structural design, I had a person
that was the subsystem manager for the forward fuselage and crew module, then another person
for the wings and the tail, and another person for the mid fuselage and aft fuselage. That’s the
way we organizationally broke it up.
    The Shuttle, as I mentioned before, was technically challenging because the thermal
protection system was something that had to be developed. The main propulsion system was
brand-new. The avionics was brand-new. We didn’t have those technologies at the start of the
program. In the Orbiter, we knew we were going to have a weight issue, because all aircraft and
any spacecraft, as it evolves, has a weight problem so you have to start with a fairly large margin
in your hip pocket. Like 20 percent at the very beginning of the program is what you’d like to
have in a weight margin, and we didn’t have it. We knew that we had a problem.
    The first thing we did is we established a design criteria, and we deviated from what [is
done for] an aircraft. Let me talk in the factor of safety: that is whatever the maximum expected
loads you can see on an aircraft, it [must] withstand 50 percent more load before it fails. [The
structure] has to be able to demonstrate that. We said, “Let’s back off instead of having a 1.5

from what was normal in the industry at that time.

Let’s think about that. We don’t really care if the material yields a little bit, as long as it doesn’t
preclude the operation of a mechanism or something of that sort, [or] causes some interference.
We can inspect it. If it yields a little bit but doesn’t fail and it’s okay to fly, let’s don’t artificially
put a factor of safety on yield,” which typically puts about a 10 percent factor on any aircraft,

just pull on a piece of metal, first thing it does is it yields. We said, “We don’t care about that as
long as it doesn’t preclude operation.” The next thing it can do is it can rupture because you just
exceed the ultimate strength capability of it. Or instead of doing that, you can put a cyclic load
on it, and it can fail during fatigue. We had to have a factor on fatigue.
    We didn’t think fatigue was an issue with the Shuttle because it didn’t have that many
flights. Each one of [the Orbiters] was designed to fly 100 times, so we said, “That’s probably
not going to be an issue. We’re not going to let that drive the weight. We’ll check it and make
sure it’s okay, but we’re not going to let that be a criteria by which we add weight to the
vehicle.”
    The other thing was fracture mechanics. That’s the fourth way something can fail is that
if a crack occurs and, depending on the type of material, it can reach a crack length where it just
lets go, and it grows very rapidly. We had to consider what fracture mechanics meant to us. We

Claude's reply:
I read all 30 pages of Odom's transcript myself and confirmed each page cite below with a phrase search. Odom never mentions Columbia, and nobody in the interview raises a concern or disagrees with anyone.

**About the accidents**
- **Challenger, p. 22**, the only passage. Asked if he was pulled back in to help: "No. And that was deliberate, because I had been a part of the project. … I was enjoined from working on the Challenger accident, which is right." On the same page he says Hubble's launch slipped when "the accident happened in January."
- **Columbia:** never mentioned. "Columbia" and "foam coming off" don't appear anywhere.
- **Closest to the debris story, p. 8:** "the orbiter tile issue came on and we had to start protecting the acreage against ice formation." The lines and brackets were then hand-insulated "to avoid chunks of ice coming off and hitting the orbiter." He presents this as a requirement that arrived and added cost. He doesn't say who raised it or that anyone pushed back; compare Sheehan pp. 5–12, where Sheehan describes fighting for that same requirement. p. 17 calls it one of "the subtle things like the additional requirements for the ice protection."
- **p. 23:** the first three tanks were painted because, out on the pad, the foam's "little minute surface [particles] will start to shed off." This is about weathering on the pad, not debris in flight. One word in it is in editorial brackets.

**Settling technical questions** (always told as design or test decisions, never as a dispute between people)
- **pp. 16–17**, the clearest case: the ground vibration test tank collapsed. "Jim, your tank just caved in" (p. 17). "It was a loading condition that we just missed when we did the structural analysis." It was fixed by keeping the tank pressurized during loading. He doesn't describe any argument over the cause or the fix.
- **p. 25:** the factor of safety was lowered to 1.25, "only 25 percent margin," justified by test data. No one is described as objecting.
- **pp. 6–7:** "We took a lot of heat in the project for the cost of the structural test program." This is pushback on spending; he calls it "the smartest money."
- **pp. 8–9, 24:** the foam had to be requalified "[about] six times" as suppliers went out of business (p. 9), and it went back through testing "six or eight times" (p. 24). This is change management, with no conflict described.
- **p. 15:** "The early tanks we shipped with a lot of open work, which [we did] not like, but to meet the schedule." It's the only hint of schedule pressure trading against quality. The next sentence, "[It was necessary.]", is entirely bracketed, so under your rule it can't be quoted as his words.
- **p. 15:** some test tanks "would go to destruction when we didn't intend for them to."
- **p. 20:** quarterly reviews before the Center Director and lab directors: "it kept us on our toes." Asked whether these were a forum for decisions: "Yes, absolutely." This is the only place a process for reviewing decisions comes up.

**Close calls that I don't count as technical concerns**
- p. 11: he "took a lot of heat" for the $7,000 full-scale tank painting.
- pp. 12–13: "a lot of angst in the system relative to Lead Center."

of that person is to interface between the Ops guys and the Engineering groups to make sure the
appropriate priorities in Engineering are established and are understood so that the operations
schedule, tasks on that schedule, can be supported and completed on time.
    That’s the day-to-day [stuff]: what does it take to recover the vehicle, safe it, inspect it,
download all the stuff from last mission, upload the new stuff, do the new checkout that’s
required, and process the vehicle on to the next stop in the flow. The vehicle manager also has to
worry about modifications that have to be done. Unfortunately, I have no earthly idea how many
modifications we did on Columbia for the first flight, but I’m guessing it had to be thousands.
There were lots of hardware at the time which wasn’t meeting its hardware development
schedules either because it just wouldn’t work or because it was slow in getting it to work.
    There was some hardware that we’d contract with vendors to deliver a particular piece,
like a nut or bolt or simple little piece of hardware, and it wouldn’t meet its specification
requirements. It was too soft or too short or too hard or too long.
    It wasn’t what we needed. So in each one of those cases the authority from the customer,
the Orbiter Project customer, the NASA customer, the change authority was in one of those
Master Change Record things I told you about earlier, the MCRs. Some project office guy in
Downey would have to write an MCR and say, “Okay, we’ve got to go get a different bolt from a
different vendor. We got to go build a different piece of hardware or a different system, a
different component.” Each one of those things would then come down here with a thing called
a mod [modification] kit which was the new piece of hardware, whether it was a nut or bolt or
flash evaporator or an APU [Auxiliary Power Unit].
    The vehicle manager would be one of the first guys down here that would be sensitive to
that [change] by communicating [daily] back with his counterpart on the West Coast. We’d

12 July 2011 28

=== PDF page 29 ===

NASA STS Recordation Oral History Project Gerald D. Sheehan

know that component X flunked or the bolts were the wrong thing or the wire was not insulated
properly or whatever the problem was. We’d know that was a forthcoming change. We’d go to
the Ops guys down here and say, “Hey, we’re going to have to change the whizbang.” Whatever
it might have been. “There’s a new mod coming. So we need to work that into your schedule.
Maybe you don’t want to do that test today because next week we’ll give you a new piece of
hardware which will invalidate all that testing. Maybe you want to do the test to make sure that
everything else around that piece of hardware works like it’s supposed to work. Then we’ll
repeat the test with the new piece of hardware after we put that in.”
Those were the kind of things that went on on a daily basis during STS-1 processing with
Columbia. It was a very, very interesting—challenging—but very interesting job. The best job I
ever had. You had nobody working for you. You were the guy responsible to make sure
everything worked. If it didn’t work, then the head guy was going to come to you and find out
what did you screw up that the right decisions weren’t made early enough in order to
accommodate whatever change was going to happen, which rolled downhill into some schedule
impact.
Part of that job also was getting the engineering requirements, all of them: the hardware
change, the test requirement change, the software change, the GSE, the ground, the facility
changes, the ICDs, everything. Putting that package together, giving it to the engineering group,
who was responsible to go implement that change in requirement or hardware or test or whatever
it was.
The engineers would go prepare implementation paper. Of course everybody used paper
then, handwritten with a black pen. Press hard, you’re making three copies on this triplicate
form. I was responsible to get those requirement packages out to the engineering groups that had

12 July 2011 29

=== PDF page 30 ===

NASA STS Recordation Oral History Project Gerald D. Sheehan

to go implement them and then collecting their work paper and taking it to the change boards.
Mainly the change board we had, because the vast majority of the stuff we did was hardware
changes which had very few test requirement or software changes associated with them, but
there were some.
    So I was the Rockwell guy that was responsible to pitch, to receive approval from the
authorizing Agency. Pitch. We had a site boss that [said] “I don’t want you guys using pitch.
That’s like you’re trying to convince somebody that you’re not doing something wrong.”
    We had to pitch the changes to the two major customer guys that were here: the KSC
head of the vehicle processing organization, the local NASA guy—that’s when we were still here
working as a processing contractor in the early days—and the JSC resident rep, who was
representing the NASA Orbiter Project Office at KSC. So I’d be responsible to know what the
change was that we had, why we were making it, what the impacts of that would be in terms of
hardware and software and test requirements. That’s why it was so important to develop that
business system ahead of time.
    So when they said, “Isn’t this going to change test procedures?” You had to have an
answer other than “Gee, I don’t know.” I’ve been there; I know that answer very well, but only
[used it] once or twice before I learned [to come with the correct, complete one].
    So I would pitch the change to Charlie [Charles B.] Mars, who was the NASA KSC guy,
and Archie [E.] Morse, who was the JSC resident office guy. I don’t think [I’m] overstating it,
[but] we had a wonderful rapport together. We understood what our jobs were; both Charlie and
Archie were old-time NASA guys that had come up through their respective organizations. I
think that was probably the [same] jobs they had during the Apollo Program. Both of them were
Apollo Spacecraft guys.

12 July 2011 30

=== PDF page 31 ===

NASA STS Recordation Oral History Project Gerald D. Sheehan

    We had a wonderful rapport together. We knew what we were supposed to do. Ninety-
nine percent of the time I was prepared. It’s always good to be prepared when you’re trying to
convince somebody to do something. That job forced me to know how all the little pieces fit
together into the big picture because those guys were experienced enough to ask questions like
what’s the impact to schedule; what’s it going to do to test requirements; why haven’t I seen
software changes that go along with this; you’re adding a new component that has a new
measurement on it, where’s the change to the data bank which tracks all the instrumentation? It
was really challenging and really satisfying kind of work.
    I’m sure I’m only remembering the good times. But boy, I can’t remember right off the
top of my head where Charlie or Archie [ever] said, “Absolutely positively no, get out of here,”
[where] I didn’t suggest ahead of time that maybe that was the answer that they should have. I
remember a couple of those where it is typical. Again, a lesson learned kind of thing for a future
program: the payload bay door linkage has little things on the ends of all the pushrods in the
mechanism called rod end bearings. It was a case of we bought a component from a vendor and
the specification requirements on the component required an ability to withstand a particular load
through that bearing. The acceptance tests of those didn’t meet it. It was way off. So my
friends in Downey invented this new MCR and designed or procured new parts and accumulated
a mod kit and sent them down here and said, “Oh, you got to.” Gave us engineering to
accomplish the [switch and] changed all those rod end bearings out. Fortunately [this] was
another case where I’d done my homework.
    Charlie, I think, asked, “Why are we doing this?”
    I said, “Same story. Part received from vendor didn’t meet the requirement.”
    He said, “I guess we got to go change it.”

NASA STS Recordation Oral History Project Gerald D. Sheehan

    I said, “Not exactly.” The spec [specification] requirement was to meet a 1,000-pound

only withstand 100 pounds. You say, holy cow, it’s only making [X %]. I was—one of the rare
times, pat myself on the back—smart enough or suspicious enough to go call the guys in
Downey and ask them just exactly what did that part see in flight.
    They said, “Oh, it’s only seeing about ten pounds.” So we had a part that was supposed
to meet X. It only met a tenth of X but that was ten times more than Y which was the load it

# Codebook: first-order concepts (Stage 2)

Concept names and definitions are the researcher's. The inclusion rules are
drafts written during coding, for the researcher to keep or revise. Examples
are exact quotes from the pages the researcher named for each concept.
Page numbers are PDF pages.

## Rules for every segment

- **Unit.** A passage by the interviewee, not the interviewer, of one to several
  consecutive sentences on one page. It describes a single episode, practice or
  reflection about how a concern or technical question was raised, handled,
  dropped or changed. Talk about the accidents counts only if it is about this.
- **Source.** Only pages included in `reading/`. The full transcripts are used
  for lookup only.
- **Quotes.** Quotes are copied exactly from the edited transcripts. Bracketed
  text is never quoted as the interviewee's words. If a passage contains
  bracketed text, the quote stops before it, or the parts on either side are
  joined with " … ". Each part is checked separately against the page.
- **Exclusion.** Mitchell p. 31, the bracketed paragraph from "[Speaking of 'what
  was going on,'" to "even if it were misguided.]", is out of the data.
- **Era** is the period the episode or practice took place in, not when it was
  told:
  - pre-Challenger: before January 1986;
  - Challenger return to flight: the investigation through STS-26 (Sept. 1988);
  - pre-Columbia: from STS-26 to February 2003;
  - Columbia return to flight: the investigation through STS-121 (2006);
  - other: after that, undated, or spanning the program.
  Uncertain eras are flagged in `coder_note`.
- **Group** is fixed per interviewee:
  - NASA manager: Smith, Mitchell, Singer;
  - NASA engineer: Pessin, Moser;
  - contractor: Blackburn, Sheehan, White.
- **One concept per row.** A passage that fits two concepts gets two rows, one
  per concept. In this pass that was done only once (Mitchell p. 38, 6 and 8).
  Other second readings are recorded in `coder_note`.
- **Uncoded.** Relevant passages that fit no concept are listed in
  `uncoded_segments.csv` with a short topic. A suggested nearby concept is given
  where one exists. The researcher decides.

## Concepts

**1. "Tell me what you think"**
- Definition: speaking your own view versus your organization's position.
- Include when: the speaker is asked for, gives, or holds back a personal
  technical judgment that differs from the position they are expected to
  represent.
- Example (Smith p. 23): "He said, “What’s your opinion?” I said, “Bob, the
  Science and Engineering position is we should pull the pump.” He said, “I want
  to know what you think.” I said, “It’s fine. It’s okay.”"

**2. "Career-limiting"**
- Definition: the cost of raising something against rank or the customer.
- Include when: the speaker describes a real or expected personal, career or
  social cost of pressing a technical point against someone senior, the
  customer, or another element.
- Example (Blackburn p. 27): "I said, “This is career-limiting, young man. You
  put this out there, besides being a laughing stock, you’re going to have some
  problems.” He refused."

**3. "They just kept probing"**
- Definition: the burden of proof sits with the person raising or defending.
- Include when: the person raising or defending a position has to prove it.
  This covers probing questions, briefings, outside review and "selling off".
- Example (Moser s2 p. 5): "The way you would convince them, or the way they
  would convince themselves that you were okay, they just kept probing and
  probing and probing and probing."

**4. "Do the test to satisfy the concern"**
- Definition: settling by test, not by agreement.
- Include when: a technical question or disagreement is settled, or meant to be
  settled, by a test, or by a flight result used as a test, rather than by
  argument or authority.
- Example (Moser s2 p. 7): "But they kept insisting and throwing up red flags,
  so we said, “Okay we’ll do the test.” … We did it to “satisfy the concern.”"
  (In the CSV this is one contiguous quote; the middle is shortened here.)

**5. "Aggressively discussing issues"**
- Definition: heated argument as normal practice.
- Include when: heated or long-running argument over a technical question is
  described as normal, legitimate or productive.
- Example (Blackburn p. 20): "I said, “No, we were aggressively discussing
  issues.” That’s the way that was at that time, and I think it was an important
  factor in terms of the successes that we had in the program."

**6. "Not my requirement"**
- Definition: each element or group owns its own requirement and passes the
  problem on.
- Include when: an element, project or group declines to own a problem or
  requirement, pushes it to another element or site, or argues over whose
  problem it is.
- Example (Sheehan p. 11): "Almost as bad as the Tank guys were, “Well, I don’t
  have a requirement to preclude ice.” So everybody was very, very parochial."

**7. "Wink-wink, nod-nod"**
- Definition: schedule and cost pressure shaping what is accepted.
- Include when: schedule, budget or flight-rate pressure is described as
  shaping what was tested, accepted or claimed.
- Example (Sheehan p. 26): "We all did “wink-wink,” “nod-nod,” “yep sure,”
  that’s the timeline."

**8. "We know about foam coming off"**
- Definition: a known anomaly treated as routine.
- Include when: a known, recurring anomaly is accepted or handled as routine or
  not a flight-safety matter.
- Example (Pessin p. 28): "The program said, “We don’t need an in-flight
  anomaly, we know about foam coming off.”"

**9. "Didn't understand the risk"**
- Definition: failure modes or effects nobody had analyzed.
- Include when: a failure mode, condition or effect had not been analyzed or
  understood (or could not be) until it happened or was investigated.
- Example (Pessin p. 27): "We, Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and JSC
  didn’t understand the failure effects of foam coming off."

**10. "I'll pass it on"**
- Definition: a concern existed but did not travel.
- Include when: a concern was voiced or written down but did not reach, or was
  not acted on by, the people who could act on it, or took a long time to be
  taken up.
- Example (Blackburn p. 29): "I looked at it and I said, “Thank you, appreciate
  that. I’ll pass it on, but I’m sure there are other people that have been
  looking at this and understand what its impact is.”"

**11. "Go back and review everything"**
- Definition: post-accident over-checking and paperwork.
- Include when: after an accident, requirements, records or analyses are
  reviewed again and paperwork grows. Pushback against this also counts.
- Example (Blackburn p. 29): "The return to flight management’s reaction to
  Challenger was every single requirement and thing that we have done is
  suspect. “You will go back and review everything you did.”"

**12. "An independent voice that could holler stop"**
- Definition: safety and quality organized apart from the project.
- Include when: safety, quality or review functions are set up or staffed apart
  from the project, or the speaker describes how the project dealt with them.
- Example (Mitchell p. 13): "They wanted to make sure that there was an
  independent voice that could holler “Stop” and make sure safety was being
  adhered to."

**13. "I believe you, but demonstrate it"**
- Definition: higher proof demanded, and permission to ask why.
- Include when: after an accident, more proof is demanded, or people are
  explicitly allowed to question settled requirements and practices.
- Example (Singer p. 15): "After Columbia, there was more effort to say, “I
  believe you, but demonstrate it.”"

**14. "This isn't the same stuff I've been spraying"**
- Definition: the person doing the work raises it.
- Include when: a technician, inspector or other hands-on worker notices a
  problem, starts a fix, or challenges a requirement.
- Example (Pessin p. 19): "The technician sprayed the 1,000-square-foot dome
  and said, “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.”"

**15. "Vendor changed it and didn't tell us"**
- Definition: hidden change upstream.
- Include when: a change by a supplier, vendor or lower-tier subcontractor that
  the program didn't know about causes or threatens a problem.
- Example (Pessin p. 21): "In this case the vendor made a change—this is again
  before we started fingerprinting—we didn’t know the change had been made, and
  he didn’t know what the effects of the change would be."

**16. "That's their decision"**
- Definition: who owns accepting risk.
- Include when: the speaker says who has the authority to accept a risk, or
  refuses to accept it and hands that to another party.
- Example (Blackburn p. 5): "So it would be up to NASA to decide whether or not
  they were going to fly under those conditions. That’s the way it was left,
  NASA assumed that risk."

**17. "One team, not us and them"**
- Definition: dissolving blame across the NASA/contractor line.
- Include when: the speaker describes trying to stop NASA–contractor blame and
  build a single team.
- Example (Smith p. 37): "This is not us and them, it’s us, all of us, Thiokol
  and the project office."

Out of the 154 rows, I'd call **40 weak or loose**. The usual problem is one of three: the quote doesn't show the concept's defining feature, it fits only through my broader inclusion rule rather than your definition, or the fit depends on context outside the quote.

**2 Career-limiting**
- SMI-12 (p. 32): the cost he fears comes from going along with a test he opposed, not from raising a concern.
- SHE-05 (p. 9): he calls it "facetious" himself, and the friction is with another element (Marshall), not with rank or the customer.

**3 They just kept probing**
- SMI-06 (p. 18): it shows him admitting "we don't know", but Beggs then accepts it without probing.
- MIT-09 (p. 26): only "a more painful day" survives in the quote; the probing itself is on p. 25, outside it.
- MOS-10 (p. 40): it's about how hard the technical problem was, not about people demanding proof.
- SMI-11 (p. 31): the NRC (National Research Council) oversight panel; it could just as well be 12.

**4 Do the test to satisfy the concern**
- MIT-06 (p. 22): a test showed a fix failed; no disagreement was being settled.
- SIN-03 (p. 9): a general statement that ground testing supports certification, not one concern being settled.
- BLA-04 (p. 12): setting up a pull-test acceptance criterion, not settling a dispute.
- WHI-08 (p. 24): it was a flight after hail damage, not a test.
- WHI-13 (p. 35): investigation tests to find the cause, not a disagreement settled by test.

**5 Aggressively discussing issues**
- BLA-07 (p. 19): he says post-Columbia leaders are "more reserved", which is the opposite of heated argument.
- MOS-07 (p. 29): the exchange with Faget is told as banter and a bet.
- MIT-07 (p. 24): "big debate", "round and round". It's persistent rather than heated; moderate fit.

**6 Not my requirement**
- MOS-14 (p. 42): it says what the tank can't do, not that anyone refused ownership or passed the problem on.
- SHE-10 (p. 23): a general point about little integration between projects; no one is shown passing a problem along.

**7 Wink-wink, nod-nod**
- MOS-11 (p. 40) and MOS2-04 (p. 5): "pacing item" names the pressure but shows nothing it shaped.
- PES-21 (p. 51): a cut schedule taken on as a challenge; nothing is shown being accepted because of it.
- WHI-09 (p. 31): schedulers misunderstanding the work, not pressure changing what was accepted.

**8 We know about foam coming off**
- MIT-15 (p. 38): background clause from a sentence double-coded with MIT-14. The anomaly is mentioned, not handled.

**9 Didn't understand the risk**
- MIT-04 (p. 18): the unknown was recognized and designed around, not overlooked until it happened.

**10 I'll pass it on**
- PES-09 (p. 28): the in-flight anomaly did reach the change board (PRCB) and was dismissed there. That arguably makes it 8, not a concern that failed to travel.
- SHE-02 (p. 6): Martin's proposal flagged icing, and the concern did travel later through Sheehan.
- BLA-06 (p. 19): an unreleased lessons-learned report, not a safety concern.
- SHE-08 (p. 13) and WHI-01 (p. 8): "hard to get taken seriously" sits on the line with 3. WHI-01 is also secondhand.

**11 Go back and review everything**
- SMI-25 (p. 38): requirements proliferation from outside bodies, not re-review.
- MIT-12 (p. 36): the normal formal certification review, not over-checking in reaction to the accident.
- BLA-15 (p. 28): an emotional reaction ("what have we done wrong"); no review is described.
- PES-19 (p. 47): a lasting process change (engineering review of all cracks), not over-checking.

**12 An independent voice that could holler stop**
- MIT-02 (p. 12): an external advisory panel, not safety or quality organized apart from the project.
- PES-16 (p. 45): engineering put onto the quality-chaired review board for nonconforming parts (MRB), so close to the reverse of the definition; your example.
- PES-20 (p. 51): an independent design-decision board, not a safety function.
- SMI-23 (p. 37): bringing Quality *into* the project office. It's a counter-instance, included only because my rule covers "how the project related to them".

**13 I believe you, but demonstrate it**
- SIN-06 (p. 12): a general statement about certifying; it doesn't mark any change after Columbia.
- SIN-05 (p. 11): secondhand, and about a "relook" leading to a redesign rather than a higher standard of proof.
- WHI-04 (p. 18) and WHI-05 (p. 19): stricter repair criteria. Neither shows more proof being demanded or permission to ask why.

**14 This isn't the same stuff I've been spraying**
- WHI-02 (p. 9) and WHI-03 (p. 10): a technician *solves* an assigned problem. That fits my "originates a fix" rule, not your "raises it".

**16 That's their decision**
- SIN-11 (p. 14): accountability for signing changes, not who accepts a risk.

# Raising and Settling Technical Concerns in the Space Shuttle Program: An Analysis of NASA Oral Histories

## Abstract

<!-- to be written after the findings -->

## Introduction

The Space Shuttle program lost two orbiters and their crews: Challenger in
January 1986 and Columbia in February 2003. This paper asks:
How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical
safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?

The two accidents give the question its structure. Each divides the program's
history into a before and an after. Between them they span most of the program's
working life, from the development years of the 1970s to its last flights in
2011. A study of how concerns were raised and settled can therefore ask what each
accident changed in that work, rather than treating the program's practice as
fixed.

The paper starts from the accounts of the people who did the work. It does not
start from the launch decisions themselves, and it does not review the writing
on them. Near the end of the program, NASA's STS Recordation Oral History
Project recorded long interviews with engineers, managers and contractor staff
who had worked on the Shuttle. The edited transcripts are public. They let the
participants describe, in their own terms, how a concern was raised, who had to
be convinced, and what happened to it.

One concept from organization research may bear on the question.
Edmondson (1999) defines team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by
members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking." Whether
and how that concept connects to raising technical concerns in the Shuttle
program is a question I return to after the findings. I do not assume a link
here.

## Data and Method

### Source and nature of the data

This is a secondary analysis of archival oral history interviews. I did not
conduct, record or transcribe any interviews. The transcripts come from NASA's
STS Recordation Oral History Project. They were downloaded as PDF files from
nasa.gov on 17 October 2026, and their SHA-256 checksums are recorded.

The interviews were conducted between April 2010 and July 2011 by the
interviewers named in each transcript: Rebecca Wright and Jennifer Ross-Nazzal,
with Sandra Johnson assisting in one Moser session. NASA's project page states
that the transcripts "are created from audio-recorded oral history interviews"
and are "presented with limited revisions," and that "Brackets and ellipses
indicate where the text has been annotated or edited for clarity." Every
transcript is headed "EDITED ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPT."

The transcripts are therefore edited records, not verbatim ones. All quotations
in this paper come from them. Bracketed text is the editors', and it is never
quoted as the interviewee's words. Where a quoted passage contains bracketed
text, the quotation stops before it, or the parts on either side are joined with
an ellipsis.

### Sample

I considered ten candidate interviews and included eight. Their roles are given
below as the transcripts themselves support them; for some interviewees these
differ from the titles on NASA's project page. Moser's two sessions (9 April and
27 May 2010) are treated as one source. They carry the header of NASA's Johnson
Space Center Oral History Project, although NASA's STS Recordation project page

The Space Shuttle program lost two orbiters and their crews: Challenger in
January 1986 (Mitchell transcript, p. 6; Moser transcript, session 1, p. 33) and
Columbia in February 2003 (Singer transcript, p. 8). This paper asks:
How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical
safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?

The two accidents give the question its structure. Each divides the program's
history into a before and an after. Between them they divide the program's working life
into three periods. A study of how concerns were raised and settled can therefore ask what each
accident changed in that work, rather than treating the program's practice as
fixed.

The paper starts from the accounts of the people who did the work. It does not
start from the launch decisions themselves, and it does not review the writing
on them. Near the end of the program, NASA's STS Recordation Oral History
Project interviewed engineers, managers and contractor staff who had worked on
the Shuttle. The edited transcripts are public. They let the
participants describe, in their own terms, how a concern was raised, who had to
be convinced, and what happened to it.

One concept from organization research may bear on the question.
Edmondson (1999) defines team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by
members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking." Whether
and how that concept connects to raising technical concerns in the Shuttle
program is a question I return to after the findings. I do not assume a link
here.

- "Aggressively discussing issues": 3 rows, 3 interviewees.

> He said, “What’s your opinion?” I said, “Bob, the Science and Engineering position is we should pull the pump.” He said, “I want to know what you think.” I said, “It’s fine. It’s okay.” So we tested, and it was okay. But my boss was very upset with me.

(Smith, p. 23; pre-Challenger; SMI-09)

(Blackburn, p. 27; pre-Challenger; BLA-13)

> We were having a very elevated, heated discussion on a technical topic. Mike can be that way, and I can be that way. (Blackburn, p. 20; pre-Challenger; BLA-08)

> The technician sprayed the 1,000-square-foot dome and said, “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.” I think he got a bonus for reporting it, hopefully he did.

(Pessin, p. 19; other; PES-03)

For "I'll pass it on" (2 rows, 2 interviewees), Blackburn describes a briefing
that an engineer on his staff brought to him the day after the Challenger

> It was a briefing that he had pitched the October before to one of the review boards about the cold temperature seal effects on the solid rocket boosters. I’ll pass it on, but I’m sure there are other people that have been looking at this and understand what its impact is.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; pre-Challenger; BLA-17)
