# Raising and Settling Technical Concerns in the Space Shuttle Program: An Analysis of NASA Oral Histories

## Abstract

<!-- to be written after the findings -->

## Introduction

The Space Shuttle program lost two orbiters and their crews: Challenger in
January 1986 (Mitchell transcript, p. 6; Moser transcript, session 1, p. 33) and
Columbia in February 2003 (Singer transcript, p. 8). This paper asks:
How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical
safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?

The two accidents give the question its structure. Each divides the program's
history into a before and an after. Between them they divide the program's working life
into three periods. A study of how concerns were raised and settled can therefore ask what each
accident changed in that work, rather than treating the program's practice as
fixed.

The paper starts from the accounts of the people who did the work. It does not
start from the launch decisions themselves, and it does not review the writing
on them. Near the end of the program, NASA's STS Recordation Oral History
Project interviewed engineers, managers and contractor staff who had worked on
the Shuttle. The edited transcripts are public. They let the
participants describe, in their own terms, how a concern was raised, who had to
be convinced, and what happened to it.

One concept from organization research may bear on the question.
Edmondson (1999) defines team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by
members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking." Whether
and how that concept connects to raising technical concerns in the Shuttle
program is a question I return to after the findings. I do not assume a link
here.

## Data and Method

### Source and nature of the data

This is a secondary analysis of archival oral history interviews. I did not
conduct, record or transcribe any interviews. The transcripts come from NASA's
STS Recordation Oral History Project. They were downloaded as PDF files from
nasa.gov on 17 October 2026, and their SHA-256 checksums are recorded.

The interviews were conducted between April 2010 and July 2011 by the
interviewers named in each transcript: Rebecca Wright and Jennifer Ross-Nazzal,
with Sandra Johnson assisting in one Moser session. NASA's project page states
that the transcripts "are created from audio-recorded oral history interviews"
and are "presented with limited revisions," and that "Brackets and ellipses
indicate where the text has been annotated or edited for clarity." Every
transcript is headed "EDITED ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPT."

The transcripts are therefore edited records, not verbatim ones. All quotations
in this paper come from them. Bracketed text is the editors', and it is never
quoted as the interviewee's words. Where a quoted passage contains bracketed
text, the quotation stops before it, or the parts on either side are joined with
an ellipsis.

### Sample

I considered ten candidate interviews and included eight. Their roles are given
below as the transcripts themselves support them; for some interviewees these
differ from the titles on NASA's project page. Moser's two sessions (9 April and
27 May 2010) are treated as one source. They carry the header of NASA's Johnson
Space Center Oral History Project, although NASA's STS Recordation project page
lists them.

| Interviewee | Interview date(s) | Role as the transcript supports it | Group |
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
| Gerald W. Smith | 12 May 2011 | NASA (Marshall). Engineer, then manager on the main engine; Solid Rocket Booster project manager after Challenger | NASA manager |
| Royce Mitchell | 30 June 2010 | NASA (Marshall). Manager of the solid rocket motor project after Challenger; later advanced solid rocket motor project manager | NASA manager |
| Jody A. Singer | 21 July 2010 | NASA (Marshall). Deputy manager, Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, to 2002; reusable solid rocket motor project manager from 2002 | NASA manager |
| Myron "Mike" A. Pessin | 30 June 2010 | NASA (Marshall), after starting as a Chrysler contractor. External Tank project engineering, then External Tank chief engineer; retired before Columbia | NASA engineer (including engineering managers) |
| Thomas L. Moser | 9 April and 27 May 2010 | NASA (Johnson). Head of structural design, responsible for the tiles before the first flight; later deputy Orbiter project manager and director of engineering | NASA engineer (including engineering managers) |
| Gerald Blackburn | 24 August 2010 | Contractor (North American Aviation / Rockwell; Boeing consultant after Columbia). Materials engineer, then head of the Materials Control and Specifications group, about 30 people | Contractor |
| Gerald D. Sheehan | 12 July 2011 | Contractor (North American / Rockwell / Boeing). Engineer; Columbia's vehicle manager at Kennedy Space Center; later ran the Project Office | Contractor |
| Terrence R. White | 12 July 2011 | Thermal protection system technician, then supervisor; employer not stated | Contractor |

Two candidates were excluded:
- **James B. Odom** barely touches either accident.
- **John W. Thomas** gives a team leader's success story with almost no raising
  of concerns or dissent. I state this exclusion openly as a limit of the study.

### Preparing the text

Claude, an AI assistant, extracted the text of each transcript page by page.
Several Claude instances each read a transcript in full and selected the page
ranges they judged relevant to raising or settling technical concerns. Those
pages were compiled, copied word for word, into excerpt files. At my request, two
further pages were added later (Pessin p. 20, Sheehan p. 19). The excerpts for
the eight sources cover 164 of their 390 transcript pages.

I read all the excerpts, including the two pages added later. Coding was applied to the excerpts only, with the full transcripts used for
lookup. I did not check what the page selection missed, so passages on pages
that were not excerpted are not in the data.

### Unit of coding

The unit of coding is a passage by the interviewee (not the interviewer) of one
to several consecutive sentences on one page. It describes a single episode,
practice or reflection about how a concern or technical question was raised,
handled, dropped or changed. Material about the accidents counts only if it is
about this. One passage is excluded from the data: a paragraph on Mitchell's
p. 31 that is set entirely in editorial brackets, which by the rule above cannot
be quoted as his words.

Each coded segment carries an era, assigned from when the episode took place:
- pre-Challenger;
- Challenger return to flight (the investigation through STS-26, September 1988);
- pre-Columbia (STS-26 to February 2003);
- Columbia return to flight (the investigation through 2006);
- other (undated or spanning the program).

Each segment also carries the interviewee's group, as in the table above.

### Coding

From my reading of the excerpts, I named 17 first-order concepts, keeping the
informants' terms where possible. Examples are "They just kept probing," "Do the
test to satisfy the concern," and "We know about foam coming off." I gave each a
one-line definition.

Claude then applied the concepts to the excerpts. It recorded each coded segment
with its exact quotation, page, era and group. Relevant passages that fit none of
the concepts were listed separately as uncoded for my decision. Claude also
drafted the inclusion rule for each concept and identified rows it judged weak or
loose fits.

I reviewed those judgments. I set aside 34 segments as weak fits, with the
one-line reason Claude had given for each, and recoded three to a different
concept. The final coding has:
- 121 coded segments;
- 34 segments set aside;
- 62 uncoded passages.

The concepts, definitions and inclusion rules are in the codebook. Four concepts
rest on a single interviewee, and two on two interviewees. I carry this into the
data structure as a limit.

### Quotation check

Every quotation was checked by a script against the extracted transcript text.
The script checks that:
- the quotation occurs on the stated page;
- it lies within the interviewee's own turn;
- it contains no bracketed text;
- it does not fall inside a bracketed editorial passage.

Where a quotation joins parts with an ellipsis, each part is checked separately
and in order. The script was itself tested on deliberately incorrect quotations
(an altered word, an interviewer's words, bracketed text, a page outside the excerpts, parts
out of order, and a passage inside the excluded Mitchell paragraph), and it
rejected each. For the representative quotations, the full transcript page was
also produced so that I could compare each quotation with its page directly.

### Data structure

I grouped the 17 concepts into five themes and the themes into three aggregate
dimensions, and named the themes and dimensions. The result is a bottom-up data
structure of first-order concepts, themes and aggregate dimensions in the style
of the Gioia approach (Gioia, Corley & Hamilton, 2013). Gioia et al. describe "a
systematic approach to new concept development and grounded theory
articulation" for inductive research. I have not yet checked the article's
requirements against my procedure.

For each theme, the data structure reports how many segments fall in each era
and each group. This shows where a theme rests on one period or one group of
informants. I chose the representative quotations.

### Who did what

- **The researcher (I):** chose the sample and the exclusions; read the excerpts;
  named the concepts, themes and dimensions; decided which segments to set aside
  or recode; chose the representative quotations; and wrote the claims of the
  model.
- **Claude:** checked names, dates and roles against the transcripts; extracted
  the text and selected the excerpt pages; applied the
  concepts to the text; drafted inclusion rules and flagged weak fits; assigned
  eras; wrote and ran the scripts for the quotation check and the data structure
  counts; verified the bibliographic records; and drafted the text of this
  paper's Introduction and Data and Method sections from the researcher's
  instructions.

## Findings

The findings are reported by aggregate dimension. Counts are coded segments
("rows") and interviewees, with Moser's two sessions counted as one interviewee.
Each quotation is copied from the coded segments. It is followed by the
interviewee, transcript page, era and segment ID.

### Dimension 1: Raising and proving concerns

Dimension 1 combines two themes:
- Theme A, "Proving it to people who keep probing": 34 rows, 8 interviewees.
- Theme B, "The price and path of speaking": 15 rows, 7 interviewees.

#### Theme A: Proving it to people who keep probing

In the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, concerns were mostly raised and
settled by the raiser proving the case to repeated probing, often by a test.
Other settlements, by trust or authority, also appear (U-MOS-17, U-MIT-20,
U-MIT-16).

The theme rests on two concepts:
- "They just kept probing": 21 rows, 6 interviewees.
- "Do the test to satisfy the concern": 13 rows, 7 interviewees.

Of the theme's 34 rows, 25 are pre-Challenger, and 11 are Moser's.

Moser describes certifying the orbiter's tiles for the first flight:

> You had to be willing to convince the people you were talking to, the decision makers, that you knew what you were doing, and you were right. The way you would convince them, or the way they would convince themselves that you were okay, they just kept probing and probing and probing and probing.

(Moser, session 2, p. 5; pre-Challenger; MOS2-03)

When outside experts asked for a wind tunnel test of the tiles, Moser's
group did not think it necessary:

> We thought, “No, we think we’ve got this covered. We understand it well enough, we understand all the loads on it, and we’ve got enough margin.” But they kept insisting and throwing up red flags, so we said, “Okay we’ll do the test.” When I say okay we’ll do the test, our project manager had to agree with it, Aaron Cohen—and Chris Kraft even agreed with it. We did it to “satisfy the concern.”

(Moser, session 2, p. 7; pre-Challenger; MOS2-05)

Three uncoded passages record other kinds of settlement. They are not quoted
here:
- an approval given on trust (U-MOS-17);
- advice, as Mitchell reports it, not to open the flawed test motor (U-MIT-20);
- a manager talked into a change (U-MIT-16).

#### Theme B: The price and path of speaking

Speaking could cost: Smith's boss was upset when he gave his own view, and
Blackburn warned a junior reviewer that a review item against the design was
career-limiting. The same theme also holds heated argument and reporting that
carried no cost or was rewarded (BLA-08, PES-03). Two interviewees, so I present
this as illustrative, not a pattern.

The theme rests on five concepts:
- "Tell me what you think": 3 rows, 1 interviewee (Smith).
- "Career-limiting": 2 rows, 1 interviewee (Blackburn), from a single episode.
- "Aggressively discussing issues": 3 rows, 3 interviewees.
- "I'll pass it on": 2 rows, 2 interviewees.
- "This isn't the same stuff I've been spraying": 5 rows, 3 interviewees.

The first two concepts each rest on a single voice.

At a meeting on a high pump torque reading, the Marshall Shuttle program
manager, Lindstrom, asked Smith what to do:

> He said, “What’s your opinion?” I said, “Bob, the Science and Engineering position is we should pull the pump.” He said, “I want to know what you think.” I said, “It’s fine. It’s okay.” So we tested, and it was okay. But my boss was very upset with me.

(Smith, p. 23; pre-Challenger; SMI-09)

Blackburn describes a young engineer from Houston who had written a review item
calling for the orbiter's circuit boards to be replaced:

> I said, “This is career-limiting, young man. You put this out there, besides being a laughing stock, you’re going to have some problems.” He refused.

(Blackburn, p. 27; pre-Challenger; BLA-13)

The same theme holds the two counter-cases named above. Blackburn on an argument
with his counterpart Mike, who had flown in from Houston:

> We were having a very elevated, heated discussion on a technical topic. Mike can be that way, and I can be that way. My secretary came in after he left and she says, “Are you going to get fired?” I said, “I don’t think so.” She said, “But you were almost at blows.” I said, “No, we were aggressively discussing issues.” That’s the way that was at that time, and I think it was an important factor in terms of the successes that we had in the program.

(Blackburn, p. 20; pre-Challenger; BLA-08)

Pessin on a technician spraying a primer that turned out to have the wrong
solvent reducer in it:

> The technician sprayed the 1,000-square-foot dome and said, “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.” I think he got a bonus for reporting it, hopefully he did.

(Pessin, p. 19; other; PES-03)

For "I'll pass it on" (2 rows, 2 interviewees), Blackburn describes a briefing
that an engineer on his staff brought to him the day after the Challenger
accident:

> It was a briefing that he had pitched the October before to one of the review boards about the cold temperature seal effects on the solid rocket boosters. Describing exactly the failure that we had. I looked at it and I said, “Thank you, appreciate that. I’ll pass it on, but I’m sure there are other people that have been looking at this and understand what its impact is.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; pre-Challenger; BLA-17)

### Dimension 2: Concerns absorbed or left unowned

Dimension 2 combines two themes:
- Theme C, "Split ownership of requirements and risk": 24 rows, 7 interviewees.
- Theme D, "Known problems absorbed as routine under pressure": 28 rows,
  7 interviewees.

#### Theme C: Split ownership of requirements and risk

Ownership of requirements and risk was split between elements (Sheehan most
clearly), and in one case between NASA and a contractor (BLA-01); problems were
passed along. Sub-tier vendor changes (Pessin, White) are a separate kind of
unowned change.

The theme rests on four concepts:
- "Not my requirement": 10 rows, 4 interviewees. Sheehan has 6 of the rows, and
  8 of the 10 are pre-Challenger.
- "Vendor changed it and didn't tell us": 8 rows, 2 interviewees (Pessin 5,
  White 3).
- "That's their decision": 4 rows, 3 interviewees. Only one row, BLA-01, is
  between NASA and a contractor.
- "One team, not us and them": 2 rows, 1 interviewee (Smith).

Sheehan, describing the period when he was seeking a requirement that the
External Tank prevent ice that could strike the orbiter:

> at the time the Orbiter guys, especially the Orbiter TPS guys working with the silica tile TPS with the reaction-cured glass coating on it, they … a “don’t touch me” kind of attitude. Almost as bad as the Tank guys were, “Well, I don’t have a requirement to preclude ice.” So everybody was very, very parochial.

(Sheehan, p. 11; pre-Challenger; SHE-06)

Sheehan on hardware designers and the launch site:

> It was kick the can down the road. … Many, many, many times I remember, “We’ll let the guys at the Cape figure that out.”

(Sheehan, p. 25; pre-Challenger; SHE-12, shortened: the opening fragment that completes a quotation from p. 24 is omitted)

Vendor changes are a separate kind. Pessin, on foam lost from the External Tank's
intertank after a supplier changed a material:

> In this case the vendor made a change—this is again before we started fingerprinting—we didn’t know the change had been made, and he didn’t know what the effects of the change would be.

(Pessin, p. 21; other; PES-05)

White, asked whether suppliers had to disclose such changes:

> No, because some of the stuff they supplied through the system, others didn’t realize that what they were changing was affecting us.

(White, p. 34; other; WHI-12)

Two parts of the data bear against this claim:
- In Sheehan's account, the program eventually recognized the anti-icing
  requirement, after he had briefed it with enough data (SHE-04).
- Smith describes a deliberate effort to build a single NASA–Thiokol team
  (SMI-20, SMI-21).

#### Theme D: Known problems absorbed as routine under pressure

Theme D is reported as two claims, M4a and M4b.

The theme rests on three concepts:
- "Wink-wink, nod-nod": 12 rows, 5 interviewees.
- "We know about foam coming off": 7 rows, 3 interviewees.
- "Didn't understand the risk": 9 rows, 7 interviewees.

**Known debris anomalies.** Known debris anomalies were handled as routine:
Pessin, with Smith and Moser s2 on the same point (SMI-19, MOS2-07). The effects
of foam loss on the orbiter had not been analyzed, by Pessin's account (concept
9: PES-06, PES-07 are Pessin's pre-Columbia account; WHI-14 is White on the
Columbia investigation test, where foam holed the wing's reinforced carbon-carbon
and the experts did not expect it; SHE-01 concerns ice debris; the other
concept-9 rows concern other problems).

Of the 7 "We know about foam coming off" rows:
- 5 are Pessin's.
- 5 are pre-Columbia, all Pessin's except SMI-19.
- Two of Pessin's rows (PES-09, PES-10) are secondhand: he had retired by then.

Pessin on how foam loss was treated with Johnson Space Center:

> Really Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and to a degree Johnson, because when we dealt with the Johnson guys foam coming off was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety.

(Pessin, p. 28; pre-Columbia; PES-08)

Pessin, secondhand, on a foam loss two flights before Columbia. The External Tank
project sent its deputy manager to the program's change board to open an

## Contribution

This paper gives a bottom-up account, drawn from eight oral histories, of how Shuttle engineers and managers say technical concerns were raised and settled, and what they say the two accidents added. Its contribution is modest and specific. First, it records, in the participants' own terms, one route a concern took in the development years: the raiser had to prove the case to repeated probing, often by a test, most clearly in the tile and structures work before the first flight. Second, it records places where a concern could lack an owner: between elements, and with sub-tier vendors who changed a material without telling the program. It also records Pessin's account of a debris anomaly handled as routine before Columbia. Third, it records what these informants say the accidents added: more checking, a separate quality organization and more paperwork after Challenger, and, from Singer alone, a higher standard of proof after Columbia. The paper does not explain either launch decision, it does not test any theory, and it makes no claim about NASA in general. I have not checked how Edmondson (1999) measures psychological safety, so I leave open whether this account connects to it.

## Limitations

The sample is eight interviews from one oral history project, chosen by me, and I excluded two (Thomas and Odom) on my own reading. The page ranges used for coding were chosen by several Claude instances, and I did not check what they missed. Claude applied my 17 concepts and drafted the inclusion rules; there was no second human coder and no test of agreement. I reviewed weak fits and set aside 34, but another reader might set aside others. Four concepts rest on one interviewee (1, 2, 13, 17), and the Columbia half of Dimension 3 is Singer alone. Only 8 of 121 rows fall between the accidents, so the paper says nothing about how practice changed in between. Much of Dimension 1 comes from the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, and most of Dimension 2's debris account is Pessin's, partly secondhand. The interviews were given in 2010 and 2011, after both accidents, and the transcripts are edited, so what the informants say may reflect hindsight and editing. I have not yet checked my procedure against what Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013) require, and I have not checked what Vaughan (1996) or Edmondson (1999) argue beyond the abstract of the latter.

# Raising and Settling Technical Concerns in the Space Shuttle Program: An Analysis of NASA Oral Histories

## Abstract

<!-- to be written after the findings -->

## Introduction

The Space Shuttle program lost two orbiters and their crews: Challenger in
January 1986 (Mitchell, 2010, p. 6; Moser, 2010a, p. 33) and
Columbia in February 2003 (Singer, 2010, p. 8). This paper asks:
How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical
safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?

The two accidents give the question its structure. Each divides the program's
history into a before and an after. Between them they divide the program's working life
into three periods. A study of how concerns were raised and settled can therefore ask what each
accident changed in that work, rather than treating the program's practice as
fixed.

The paper starts from the accounts of the people who did the work. It does not
start from the launch decisions themselves, and it does not review the writing
on them. Near the end of the program, NASA's STS Recordation Oral History
Project interviewed engineers, managers and contractor staff who had worked on
the Shuttle. The edited transcripts are public. They let the
participants describe, in their own terms, how a concern was raised, who had to
be convinced, and what happened to it.

One concept from organization research may bear on the question.
Edmondson (1999) defines team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by
members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking." Whether
and how that concept connects to raising technical concerns in the Shuttle
program is a question I return to after the findings. I do not assume a link
here.

## Data and Method

### Source and nature of the data

This is a secondary analysis of archival oral history interviews; I did not
conduct, record or transcribe any. The transcripts come from NASA's STS
Recordation Oral History Project and were downloaded as PDF files from nasa.gov
on 17 October 2026, with their SHA-256 checksums recorded. The interviews were
conducted between April 2010 and July 2011 by the interviewers named in each
transcript: Rebecca Wright and Jennifer Ross-Nazzal, with Sandra Johnson
assisting in one Moser session. NASA's project page states that the transcripts
"are created from audio-recorded oral history interviews" and are "presented
with limited revisions," and that "Brackets and ellipses indicate where the text
has been annotated or edited for clarity." Every transcript is headed "EDITED
ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPT."

The transcripts are therefore edited, not verbatim, records. All quotations come
from them. Bracketed text is the editors' and is never quoted as the
interviewee's words. Where a quoted passage contains bracketed text, the
quotation stops before it, or joins the parts on either side with an ellipsis.

### Sample

I considered ten candidate interviews and included eight (Table 1). Roles are
given as the transcripts support them, which for some interviewees differs from
the titles on NASA's project page. Moser's two sessions (9 April and 27 May 2010)
are treated as one source. They carry the header of NASA's Johnson Space Center
Oral History Project, although NASA's STS Recordation project page lists them.
In the Group column, "NASA engineer" includes engineering managers.

Table 1. Sample.

| Interviewee | Date(s) | Role as the transcript supports it | Group |
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
| Gerald W. Smith | 12 May 2011 | NASA (Marshall): main engine engineer, then manager; Solid Rocket Booster project manager after Challenger | NASA manager |
| Royce Mitchell | 30 June 2010 | NASA (Marshall): solid rocket motor project manager after Challenger; later advanced solid rocket motor project manager | NASA manager |
| Jody A. Singer | 21 July 2010 | NASA (Marshall): deputy manager, Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, to 2002; reusable solid rocket motor project manager from 2002 | NASA manager |
| Myron "Mike" A. Pessin | 30 June 2010 | NASA (Marshall), after starting as a Chrysler contractor: External Tank project engineering, then chief engineer; retired before Columbia | NASA engineer |
| Thomas L. Moser | 9 April, 27 May 2010 | NASA (Johnson): head of structural design, responsible for the tiles before the first flight; later deputy Orbiter project manager, director of engineering | NASA engineer |
| Gerald Blackburn | 24 August 2010 | Contractor (North American Aviation / Rockwell; Boeing consultant after Columbia): materials engineer, then head of the Materials Control and Specifications group, about 30 people | Contractor |
| Gerald D. Sheehan | 12 July 2011 | Contractor (North American / Rockwell / Boeing): engineer; Columbia's vehicle manager at Kennedy Space Center; later ran the Project Office | Contractor |
| Terrence R. White | 12 July 2011 | Thermal protection system technician, then supervisor; employer not stated | Contractor |

I excluded two candidates:
- **James B. Odom** barely touches either accident.
- **John W. Thomas** gives a team leader's success story with almost no raising
  of concerns or dissent. I state this exclusion openly as a limit of the study.

### Preparing the text

Claude, an AI assistant, extracted each transcript's text page by page. Several
Claude instances each read a transcript in full and selected the page ranges
they judged relevant to raising or settling technical concerns. Those pages were
copied word for word into excerpt files. Two further pages were added later at
my request (Pessin p. 20, Sheehan p. 19). The excerpts cover 164 of the eight
sources' 390 transcript pages. I read all the excerpts, including the two pages added later. Coding was applied to the excerpts only, with the
full transcripts used for lookup.

### Unit of coding

The unit of coding is a passage by the interviewee (not the interviewer) of one
to several consecutive sentences on one page. It describes a single episode,
practice or reflection about how a concern or technical question was raised,
handled, dropped or changed. Material about the accidents counts only if it is
about this. One passage is excluded: a paragraph on Mitchell's p. 31 set
entirely in editorial brackets, which by the rule above cannot be quoted as his
words.

Each coded segment carries the interviewee's group (Table 1) and an era, assigned
from when the episode took place:
- pre-Challenger;
- Challenger return to flight (the investigation through STS-26, September 1988);
- pre-Columbia (STS-26 to February 2003);
- Columbia return to flight (the investigation through 2006);
- other (undated or spanning the program).

### Coding

From my reading of the excerpts, I named 17 first-order concepts and gave each a
one-line definition. I kept the informants' terms where possible: for example,
"They just kept probing," "Do the test to satisfy the concern" and "We know
about foam coming off."

Claude applied the concepts to the excerpts. It recorded each coded segment with
its exact quotation, page, era and group, and listed relevant passages that fit
no concept as uncoded, for my decision. Claude also drafted an inclusion rule
for each concept and flagged rows it judged weak or loose fits.

I set aside 34 segments as weak fits, with the one-line reason Claude had given
for each, and recoded three. The final coding has 121 coded segments, 34 set
aside and 62 uncoded passages. The concepts, definitions and inclusion rules are
in the codebook.

### Quotation check

A script checked every quotation against the extracted transcript text. It
checks that each quotation:
- occurs on the stated page;
- lies within the interviewee's own turn;
- contains no bracketed text;
- does not fall inside a bracketed editorial passage.

Parts joined by an ellipsis are checked separately and in order. The script was
itself tested on deliberately incorrect quotations, and it rejected each: an
altered word, an interviewer's words, bracketed text, a page outside the
excerpts, parts out of order, and a passage inside the excluded Mitchell
paragraph. For the representative quotations, the full transcript page was also
produced so that I could compare each quotation with its page.

### Data structure

I grouped the 17 concepts into five themes and the themes into three aggregate
dimensions, and named the themes and dimensions. The result is a bottom-up data
structure of first-order concepts, themes and aggregate dimensions in the style
of the Gioia approach (Gioia et al., 2013). It is shown in Table 2, at the start
of the Findings. Gioia et al. describe "a systematic approach to new concept
development and grounded theory articulation" for inductive research. I have
not yet checked the article's requirements against my procedure.

The full data structure in the project files also reports, for each theme, how
many segments fall in each era and each group. This shows where a theme rests on
one period or one group of informants. I chose the representative quotations.

### Who did what

- **The researcher (I):** chose the sample and the exclusions; read the excerpts;
  named the concepts, themes and dimensions; decided which segments to set aside
  or recode; chose the representative quotations; and wrote the claims of the
  model.
- **Claude:** checked names, dates and roles against the transcripts; extracted
  the text and selected the excerpt pages; applied the concepts; drafted
  inclusion rules and flagged weak fits; assigned eras; wrote and ran the
  quotation-check and counting scripts; verified the bibliographic records; and
  drafted the Introduction, Data and Method, and Findings from the researcher's
  instructions.

## Findings

The findings are reported by aggregate dimension. Counts are coded segments
("rows") and interviewees, with Moser's two sessions counted as one interviewee.
Each quotation is copied from the coded segments. It is followed by the
interviewee, transcript page, era and segment ID. Table 2 gives the data
structure, with the rows and interviewees for each concept. ⚠ marks a concept
that rests on a single interviewee.

Table 2. Data structure.

| Dimension | Theme | Concept | Rows | Interviewees |
|:-|:-|:-|-:|-:|
| 1. Raising and proving concerns (49 rows, 8 interviewees) | A. Proving it to people who keep probing (34, 8) | They just kept probing | 21 | 6 |
|  |  | Do the test to satisfy the concern | 13 | 7 |
|  | B. The price and path of speaking (15, 7) | Tell me what you think ⚠ | 3 | 1 |
|  |  | Career-limiting ⚠ | 2 | 1 |
|  |  | Aggressively discussing issues | 3 | 3 |
|  |  | I'll pass it on | 2 | 2 |
|  |  | This isn't the same stuff I've been spraying | 5 | 3 |
| 2. Concerns absorbed or left unowned (52 rows, 7 interviewees) | C. Split ownership of requirements and risk (24, 7) | Not my requirement | 10 | 4 |
|  |  | Vendor changed it and didn't tell us | 8 | 2 |
|  |  | That's their decision | 4 | 3 |
|  |  | One team, not us and them ⚠ | 2 | 1 |
|  | D. Known problems absorbed as routine under pressure (28, 7) | Wink-wink, nod-nod | 12 | 5 |
|  |  | We know about foam coming off | 7 | 3 |
|  |  | Didn't understand the risk | 9 | 7 |
| 3. What the accidents added to the work (20 rows, 6 interviewees) | E. What the accidents added: more checking, separate oversight, licence to ask why (20, 6) | Go back and review everything | 9 | 5 |
|  |  | An independent voice that could holler stop | 4 | 3 |
|  |  | I believe you, but demonstrate it ⚠ | 7 | 1 |

### Dimension 1: Raising and proving concerns

#### Theme A: Proving it to people who keep probing

In the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, concerns were mostly raised and
settled by the raiser proving the case to repeated probing, often by a test.
Other settlements, by trust or authority, also appear (U-MOS-17, U-MIT-20,
U-MIT-16).

Of the theme's 34 rows, 25 are pre-Challenger, and 11 are Moser's.

Moser describes certifying the orbiter's tiles for the first flight:

> You had to be willing to convince the people you were talking to, the decision makers, that you knew what you were doing, and you were right. The way you would convince them, or the way they would convince themselves that you were okay, they just kept probing and probing and probing and probing.

(Moser, session 2, p. 5; pre-Challenger; MOS2-03)

When outside experts asked for a wind tunnel test of the tiles, Moser's
group did not think it necessary:

> We thought, “No, we think we’ve got this covered. We understand it well enough, we understand all the loads on it, and we’ve got enough margin.” But they kept insisting and throwing up red flags, so we said, “Okay we’ll do the test.” When I say okay we’ll do the test, our project manager had to agree with it, Aaron Cohen—and Chris Kraft even agreed with it. We did it to “satisfy the concern.”

(Moser, session 2, p. 7; pre-Challenger; MOS2-05)

Three uncoded passages record other kinds of settlement. They are not quoted
here:
- an approval given on trust (U-MOS-17);
- advice, as Mitchell reports it, not to open the flawed test motor (U-MIT-20);
- a manager talked into a change (U-MIT-16).

#### Theme B: The price and path of speaking

Speaking could cost: Smith's boss was upset when he gave his own view, and
Blackburn warned a junior reviewer that a review item against the design was
career-limiting. The same theme also holds heated argument and reporting that
carried no cost or was rewarded (BLA-08, PES-03). Two interviewees, so I present
this as illustrative, not a pattern.

"Tell me what you think" is Smith's alone, and "Career-limiting" is
Blackburn's alone, from a single episode.

At a meeting on a high pump torque reading, the Marshall Shuttle program
manager, Lindstrom, asked Smith what to do:

> He said, “What’s your opinion?” I said, “Bob, the Science and Engineering position is we should pull the pump.” He said, “I want to know what you think.” I said, “It’s fine. It’s okay.” So we tested, and it was okay. But my boss was very upset with me.

(Smith, p. 23; pre-Challenger; SMI-09)

Blackburn describes a young engineer from Houston who had written a review item
calling for the orbiter's circuit boards to be replaced:

> I said, “This is career-limiting, young man. You put this out there, besides being a laughing stock, you’re going to have some problems.” He refused.

(Blackburn, p. 27; pre-Challenger; BLA-13)

The same theme holds the two counter-cases named above. Blackburn on an argument
with his counterpart Mike, who had flown in from Houston:

> We were having a very elevated, heated discussion on a technical topic. Mike can be that way, and I can be that way. My secretary came in after he left and she says, “Are you going to get fired?” I said, “I don’t think so.” She said, “But you were almost at blows.” I said, “No, we were aggressively discussing issues.” That’s the way that was at that time, and I think it was an important factor in terms of the successes that we had in the program.

(Blackburn, p. 20; pre-Challenger; BLA-08)

Pessin on a technician spraying a primer that turned out to have the wrong
solvent reducer in it:

> The technician sprayed the 1,000-square-foot dome and said, “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.” I think he got a bonus for reporting it, hopefully he did.

(Pessin, p. 19; other; PES-03)

For "I'll pass it on", Blackburn describes a briefing
that an engineer on his staff brought to him the day after the Challenger
accident:

> It was a briefing that he had pitched the October before to one of the review boards about the cold temperature seal effects on the solid rocket boosters. Describing exactly the failure that we had. I looked at it and I said, “Thank you, appreciate that. I’ll pass it on, but I’m sure there are other people that have been looking at this and understand what its impact is.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; pre-Challenger; BLA-17)

### Dimension 2: Concerns absorbed or left unowned

#### Theme C: Split ownership of requirements and risk

Ownership of requirements and risk was split between elements (Sheehan most
clearly), and in one case between NASA and a contractor (BLA-01); problems were
passed along. Sub-tier vendor changes (Pessin, White) are a separate kind of
unowned change.

Four details are not in Table 2:
- Sheehan has 6 of the 10 "Not my requirement" rows, and 8 of the 10 are
  pre-Challenger.
- The vendor rows are Pessin's (5) and White's (3).
- Of the "That's their decision" rows, only BLA-01 is between NASA and a
  contractor.
- "One team, not us and them" is Smith's alone.

Sheehan, describing the period when he was seeking a requirement that the
External Tank prevent ice that could strike the orbiter:

> at the time the Orbiter guys, especially the Orbiter TPS guys working with the silica tile TPS with the reaction-cured glass coating on it, they … a “don’t touch me” kind of attitude. Almost as bad as the Tank guys were, “Well, I don’t have a requirement to preclude ice.” So everybody was very, very parochial.

(Sheehan, p. 11; pre-Challenger; SHE-06)

Sheehan on hardware designers and the launch site:

> It was kick the can down the road. … Many, many, many times I remember, “We’ll let the guys at the Cape figure that out.”

(Sheehan, p. 25; pre-Challenger; SHE-12, shortened: the opening fragment that completes a quotation from p. 24 is omitted)

Vendor changes are a separate kind. Pessin, on foam lost from the External Tank's
intertank after a supplier changed a material:

> In this case the vendor made a change—this is again before we started fingerprinting—we didn’t know the change had been made, and he didn’t know what the effects of the change would be.

(Pessin, p. 21; other; PES-05)

White, asked whether suppliers had to disclose such changes:

> No, because some of the stuff they supplied through the system, others didn’t realize that what they were changing was affecting us.

(White, p. 34; other; WHI-12)

Two parts of the data bear against this claim:
- In Sheehan's account, the program eventually recognized the anti-icing
  requirement, after he had briefed it with enough data (SHE-04).
- Smith describes a deliberate effort to build a single NASA–Thiokol team
  (SMI-20, SMI-21).

#### Theme D: Known problems absorbed as routine under pressure

Theme D is reported as two claims: a debris claim (known debris anomalies) and a
pressure claim (schedule and cost pressure).

**Known debris anomalies.** Known debris anomalies were handled as routine:
Pessin, with Smith and Moser s2 on the same point (SMI-19, MOS2-07). The effects
of foam loss on the orbiter had not been analyzed, by Pessin's account (concept
9: PES-06, PES-07 are Pessin's pre-Columbia account; WHI-14 is White on the
Columbia investigation test, where foam holed the wing's reinforced carbon-carbon
and the experts did not expect it; SHE-01 concerns ice debris; the other
concept-9 rows concern other problems).

Of the 7 "We know about foam coming off" rows:
- 5 are Pessin's.
- 5 are pre-Columbia, all Pessin's except SMI-19.
- Two of Pessin's rows (PES-09, PES-10) are secondhand: he had retired by then.

Pessin on how foam loss was treated with Johnson Space Center:

> Really Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and to a degree Johnson, because when we dealt with the Johnson guys foam coming off was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety.

(Pessin, p. 28; pre-Columbia; PES-08)

Pessin, secondhand, on a foam loss two flights before Columbia. The External Tank
project sent its deputy manager to the program's change board to open an
in-flight anomaly:

> The program said, “We don’t need an in-flight anomaly, we know about foam coming off.” The program manager turned to the ET project manager and said, “Do a study to see what you can do to improve it.”

(Pessin, p. 28; pre-Columbia; PES-10)

Pessin on the External Tank engineering:

> But one thing that we, Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, didn’t do was a technique called process deviation analysis. … What we didn’t do—and I say we, Marshall engineering, we, Martin engineering—we didn’t really understand the process failure modes. We, Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and JSC didn’t understand the failure effects of foam coming off. … All of us didn’t understand the risk, but as far as the process—we certified spray technicians.

(Pessin, p. 27; pre-Columbia; PES-06)

Two rows in the same evidence are attempts to stop the routinizing:
- Moser told a tile engineer that debris impact could not simply be declared
  acceptable, and set out three choices (MOS2-08).
- The External Tank project's deputy tried to open an in-flight anomaly (PES-09).

**Schedule and cost pressure.** Schedule and cost pressure shaped what was tested
and accepted, mostly in pre-Challenger tile, structures and engine work (concept
7).

Of the 12 "Wink-wink, nod-nod" rows, 10 are pre-Challenger:
- tile and structures: Moser, 5 rows;
- engine: Smith, 2 rows;
- orbiter changes: Blackburn, 1 row;
- processing timelines: Sheehan, 2 rows.

The other 2 are from the Challenger return to flight (Smith, Mitchell).

Sheehan on the planned turnaround time for the orbiter between flights:

> We all did “wink-wink,” “nod-nod,” “yep sure,” that’s the timeline. But that’s the timeline that was required to get the mission model to get the launch flight rate to get the cost per pound figures that the Agency was using with the Congress to show how cheap and efficient Shuttle was going to be.

(Sheehan, p. 26; pre-Challenger; SHE-13)

The claim rests partly on speakers who themselves say safety was not
compromised. Moser, on the structural test program cut back for budget:

> Had we had the money that we set the program out with, we wouldn’t have done this, but we did not compromise safety at all.

(Moser, session 1, p. 24; pre-Challenger; MOS-06)

**The two claims are not linked in the data.** The data does not link the debris claim
to the pressure claim. No "We know about foam coming off" quotation mentions schedule, cost or
pressure, and no "Wink-wink, nod-nod" row is about debris.

#### A synthesis across Themes C and D

*Researcher's synthesis, not a coded finding.*

Read together, the ownership claim (Theme C) and the debris claim describe how a concern could exist and still not be
owned or acted on. No row is coded to both a Theme C and a Theme D concept. On
three pages, concepts from the two themes are coded side by side:
- **Smith p. 35:** finger pointing over where debris came from (SMI-18), next to
  the External Tank project's rationale that nothing large enough to cause a
  problem would come off (SMI-19).
- **Moser session 2, p. 10:** a push to say debris impact was acceptable
  (MOS2-07), next to Moser's statement of who may accept that risk (MOS2-08).
- **Sheehan p. 26:** designers leaving test and checkout questions to the launch
  site (SHE-14), next to the turnaround timeline that he and others knew would
  not be met (SHE-13). This page pairs a Theme C concept with the pressure claim, not
  the debris claim.

The concept "I'll pass it on" (in Theme B) also bears on a concern
existing without being acted on.

In a counter-case, Sheehan's anti-icing concern was passed between elements and
was eventually taken up as a program requirement after briefings (SHE-04).

### Dimension 3: What the accidents added to the work

Dimension 3 has one theme: Theme E, "What the accidents added: more checking,
separate oversight, licence to ask why". The theme has no pre-Challenger or pre-Columbia rows. Its rows by era:
- Challenger return to flight: 11 rows (Smith 4, Pessin 3, Mitchell 2, Blackburn
  1, White 1).
- Columbia return to flight: 8 rows, all Singer's.
- Other: 1 row (White).

After Challenger, practice added checking, separate quality/safety
organization, and paperwork ("Go back and review everything"; "An independent
voice that could holler stop"). After Columbia, one informant, Singer, reports a
higher proof standard and licence to ask why ("I believe you, but demonstrate
it").

The separate-organization point rests on:
- Mitchell's account of the Rogers Commission requirement (MIT-01, MIT-03);
- Smith's objection to how Quality's independence worked (SMI-22);
- Pessin on an outside-led review (PES-18).

By concept:
- **"Go back and review everything":** 7 rows are from the Challenger return to
  flight, 1 from the Columbia return to flight (Singer) and 1 is undated (White).
- **"An independent voice that could holler stop":** all rows are from the
  Challenger return to flight.
- **"I believe you, but demonstrate it":** all rows (Singer's) are from the
  Columbia return to flight.

Blackburn on the return to flight after Challenger:

> The return to flight management’s reaction to Challenger was every single requirement and thing that we have done is suspect. “You will go back and review everything you did.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; Challenger return to flight; BLA-16)

Smith on the design reviews for the redesigned solid rocket motor, in which
reviewers wrote up review item discrepancies (RIDs):

> Needless to say, the engineering community post-Challenger was very risk-averse. If it was something that they had any responsibility for, they would write it up. As a consequence there were thousands of RIDs generated in these reviews.

(Smith, p. 33; Challenger return to flight; SMI-16)

Smith on the separate Safety and Mission Assurance organization:

> After the Challenger accident, a deputy administrator for Safety and Mission Assurance was established. The big push then was the independence of the Quality people from the project, which I had a problem with. Not the independence, but I had Quality people sitting down in another building critiquing what we’re doing, and all I got was notes, “This is a problem; this is a problem.”

(Smith, p. 37; Challenger return to flight; SMI-22)

Singer, asked whether attitudes toward safety changed after Columbia:

> Before there may have been more of an acceptance that an element had done their homework and it was safe to fly. After Columbia, there was more effort to say, “I believe you, but demonstrate it.”

(Singer, p. 15; Columbia return to flight; SIN-12)

The data also holds additions that were resisted or reversed, and checking that
thinned out. White on the repair paperwork added after Challenger:

> Basically they wanted a lot more, and it took us a long time to convince them that they didn’t need that. We eventually convinced them, “Look. We’re doing thousands of repairs. What are you doing with all this data?” And they admitted they weren’t doing anything, so we convinced them to let us go undocumented.

(White, p. 49; other; WHI-18)

The other two cases are:
- **Smith's objection** (SMI-22, above): critique from Quality arrived as notes
  from another building.
- **An uncoded passage from Blackburn** (U-BLA-29): when he returned after
  Columbia, the per-flight material checks once handled by his staff of about
  five were signed off by one person.

## Contribution

This paper gives a bottom-up account, drawn from eight oral histories, of how Shuttle engineers and managers say technical concerns were raised and settled, and what they say the two accidents added. Its contribution is modest and specific. First, it records, in the participants' own terms, one route a concern took in the development years: the raiser had to prove the case to repeated probing, often by a test, most clearly in the tile and structures work before the first flight. Second, it records places where a concern could lack an owner: between elements, and with sub-tier vendors who changed a material or its process without telling the program. It also records Pessin's account of a debris anomaly handled as routine before Columbia. Third, it records what these informants say the accidents added: more checking, a separate quality organization and more paperwork after Challenger, and, from Singer alone, a higher standard of proof after Columbia. The paper does not explain either launch decision, it does not test any theory, and it makes no claim about NASA in general. I have not checked how Edmondson (1999) measures psychological safety, so I leave open whether this account connects to it.

## Limitations

The sample is eight interviewees, nine transcripts, from NASA's oral history programme: seven interviewees from the STS Recordation Oral History Project, and Moser's two sessions, which carry the Johnson Space Center Oral History Project header. I chose them, and I excluded two: Thomas, on my own reading of his transcript, and Odom, on Claude's page-cited reading of his whole transcript. The page ranges used for coding were chosen by several Claude instances, and I did not check what they missed. Claude applied my 17 concepts and drafted the inclusion rules; there was no second human coder and no test of agreement. I reviewed weak fits and set aside 34, but another reader might set aside others. Four concepts rest on one interviewee (1, 2, 13, 17), and the Columbia half of Dimension 3 is Singer alone. Only 8 of 121 rows fall between the 1988 return to flight and Columbia, so the paper says little about how practice changed in those years. Dimension 1's strongest support is the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, which is the part of it I describe most firmly, and most of Dimension 2's debris account is Pessin's, partly secondhand. The interviews were given in 2010 and 2011, after both accidents, and the transcripts are edited, so what the informants say may reflect hindsight and editing. I have not yet checked my procedure against what Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013) require, and I have not checked what Vaughan or Edmondson argue beyond the abstract of Edmondson (1999).

## References

Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. *Administrative Science Quarterly, 44*(2), 350–383. https://doi.org/10.2307/2666999

Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. *Organizational Research Methods, 16*(1), 15–31. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428112452151

## Sources

The data are nine edited oral history transcripts, downloaded as PDF files on 17 October 2026. In-text citations of a transcript use the key shown in bold. Quotations in the Findings are attributed by interviewee and transcript page; for Moser, "session 1" is Moser (2010a) and "session 2" is Moser (2010b). # Raising and Settling Technical Concerns in the Space Shuttle Program: An Analysis of NASA Oral Histories

## Abstract

This paper asks how engineers and managers in the Space Shuttle program raised
and handled technical safety concerns, and how the Challenger and Columbia
accidents changed those practices. It is a secondary analysis of nine edited
oral history transcripts from eight interviewees, recorded in 2010 and 2011 for
NASA's oral history projects. I named 17 first-order concepts from my reading.
Claude, an AI assistant, applied them to transcript excerpts, and a script
checked every quotation against the transcript text.

Findings:
- In the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, concerns were mostly raised and
  settled by the raiser proving the case to repeated probing, often by a test.
- Ownership of requirements and risk was split between elements, and problems
  were passed along.
- Known debris anomalies were handled as routine (Pessin, with Smith and Moser on
  the same point).
- After Challenger, practice added checking, separate quality/safety
  organization, and paperwork.
- After Columbia, one informant, Singer, reports a higher proof standard and
  licence to ask why.

The evidence is thin between the 1988 return to flight and Columbia: 8 of 121
coded segments.

## Introduction

The Space Shuttle program lost two orbiters and their crews: Challenger in
January 1986 (Mitchell, 2010, p. 6; Moser, 2010a, p. 33) and
Columbia in February 2003 (Singer, 2010, p. 8). This paper asks:
How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical
safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?

The two accidents give the question its structure. Each divides the program's
history into a before and an after. Between them they divide the program's working life
into three periods. A study of how concerns were raised and settled can therefore ask what each
accident changed in that work, rather than treating the program's practice as
fixed.

The paper starts from the accounts of the people who did the work. It does not
start from the launch decisions themselves, and it does not review the writing
on them. Near the end of the program, NASA's STS Recordation Oral History
Project interviewed engineers, managers and contractor staff who had worked on
the Shuttle. The edited transcripts are public. They let the
participants describe, in their own terms, how a concern was raised, who had to
be convinced, and what happened to it.

One concept from organization research may bear on the question.
Edmondson (1999) defines team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by
members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking." Whether
and how that concept connects to raising technical concerns in the Shuttle
program is a question I return to after the findings. I do not assume a link
here.

## Data and Method

### Source and nature of the data

This is a secondary analysis of archival oral history interviews; I did not
conduct, record or transcribe any. The transcripts come from NASA's STS
Recordation Oral History Project and were downloaded as PDF files from nasa.gov
on 17 October 2026, with their SHA-256 checksums recorded. The interviews were
conducted between April 2010 and July 2011 by the interviewers named in each
transcript: Rebecca Wright and Jennifer Ross-Nazzal, with Sandra Johnson
assisting in one Moser session. NASA's project page states that the transcripts
"are created from audio-recorded oral history interviews" and are "presented
with limited revisions," and that "Brackets and ellipses indicate where the text
has been annotated or edited for clarity." Every transcript is headed "EDITED
ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPT."

The transcripts are therefore edited, not verbatim, records. All quotations come
from them. Bracketed text is the editors' and is never quoted as the
interviewee's words. Where a quoted passage contains bracketed text, the
quotation stops before it, or joins the parts on either side with an ellipsis.

given as the transcripts support them, which for some interviewees differs from
the titles on NASA's project page. Moser's two sessions (9 April and 27 May 2010)
are treated as one source. They carry the header of NASA's Johnson Space Center
Oral History Project, although NASA's STS Recordation project page lists them.
In the Group column, "NASA engineer" includes engineering managers.

### Preparing the text

Claude, an AI assistant, extracted each transcript's text page by page. Several
Claude instances each read a transcript in full and selected the page ranges
they judged relevant to raising or settling technical concerns. Those pages were
copied word for word into excerpt files. Two further pages were added later at
my request (Pessin p. 20, Sheehan p. 19). The excerpts cover 164 of the eight
sources' 390 transcript pages. I read all the excerpts, including the two pages added later. Coding was applied to the excerpts only, with the
full transcripts used for lookup.

### Unit of coding

The unit of coding is a passage by the interviewee (not the interviewer) of one
to several consecutive sentences on one page. It describes a single episode,
practice or reflection about how a concern or technical question was raised,
handled, dropped or changed. Material about the accidents counts only if it is
about this. One passage is excluded: a paragraph on Mitchell's p. 31 set
entirely in editorial brackets, which by the rule above cannot be quoted as his
words.

Each coded segment carries the interviewee's group (Table 1) and an era, assigned
from when the episode took place:
- pre-Challenger;
- Challenger return to flight (the investigation through STS-26, September 1988);
- pre-Columbia (STS-26 to February 2003);
- Columbia return to flight (the investigation through 2006);
- other (undated or spanning the program).

### Coding

From my reading of the excerpts, I named 17 first-order concepts and gave each a
one-line definition. I kept the informants' terms where possible: for example,
"They just kept probing," "Do the test to satisfy the concern" and "We know
about foam coming off."

Claude applied the concepts to the excerpts. It recorded each coded segment with
its exact quotation, page, era and group, and listed relevant passages that fit
no concept as uncoded, for my decision. Claude also drafted an inclusion rule
for each concept and flagged rows it judged weak or loose fits.

I set aside 34 segments as weak fits, with the one-line reason Claude had given
for each, and recoded three. The final coding has 121 coded segments, 34 set
aside and 62 uncoded passages. The concepts, definitions and inclusion rules are
in the codebook.

### Quotation check

A script checked every quotation against the extracted transcript text. It
checks that each quotation:
- occurs on the stated page;
- lies within the interviewee's own turn;
- contains no bracketed text;
- does not fall inside a bracketed editorial passage.

Parts joined by an ellipsis are checked separately and in order. The script was
itself tested on deliberately incorrect quotations, and it rejected each: an
altered word, an interviewer's words, bracketed text, a page outside the
excerpts, parts out of order, and a passage inside the excluded Mitchell
paragraph. For the representative quotations, the full transcript page was also
produced so that I could compare each quotation with its page.

### Data structure

I grouped the 17 concepts into five themes and the themes into three aggregate
dimensions, and named the themes and dimensions. The result is a bottom-up data
structure of first-order concepts, themes and aggregate dimensions in the style
of the Gioia approach (Gioia et al., 2013). It is shown in Table 2, at the start
of the Findings. Gioia et al. describe "a systematic approach to new concept
development and grounded theory articulation" for inductive research. I have
not yet checked the article's requirements against my procedure.

The full data structure in the project files also reports, for each theme, how
many segments fall in each era and each group. This shows where a theme rests on
one period or one group of informants. I chose the representative quotations.

### Who did what

- **The researcher (I):** chose the sample and the exclusions; read the excerpts;
  named the concepts, themes and dimensions; decided which segments to set aside
  or recode; chose the representative quotations; and wrote the claims of the
  model.
- **Claude:** checked names, dates and roles against the transcripts; extracted
  the text and selected the excerpt pages; applied the concepts; drafted
  inclusion rules and flagged weak fits; assigned eras; wrote and ran the
  quotation-check and counting scripts; verified the bibliographic records; and
  drafted the Introduction, Data and Method, and Findings from the researcher's
  instructions.

### Dimension 1: Raising and proving concerns

#### Theme A: Proving it to people who keep probing

In the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, concerns were mostly raised and
settled by the raiser proving the case to repeated probing, often by a test.
Other settlements, by trust or authority, also appear (U-MOS-17, U-MIT-20,
U-MIT-16).

Of the theme's 34 rows, 25 are pre-Challenger, and 11 are Moser's.

Moser describes certifying the orbiter's tiles for the first flight:

> You had to be willing to convince the people you were talking to, the decision makers, that you knew what you were doing, and you were right. The way you would convince them, or the way they would convince themselves that you were okay, they just kept probing and probing and probing and probing.

(Moser, session 2, p. 5; pre-Challenger; MOS2-03)

When outside experts asked for a wind tunnel test of the tiles, Moser's
group did not think it necessary:

> But they kept insisting and throwing up red flags, so we said, “Okay we’ll do the test.” … We did it to “satisfy the concern.”

(Moser, session 2, p. 7; pre-Challenger; MOS2-05, shortened)

Three uncoded passages record other kinds of settlement. They are not quoted
here:
- an approval given on trust (U-MOS-17);
- advice, as Mitchell reports it, not to open the flawed test motor (U-MIT-20);
- a manager talked into a change (U-MIT-16).

#### Theme B: The price and path of speaking

Speaking could cost: Smith's boss was upset when he gave his own view, and
Blackburn warned a junior reviewer that a review item against the design was
career-limiting. The same theme also holds heated argument and reporting that
carried no cost or was rewarded (BLA-08, PES-03). Two interviewees, so I present
this as illustrative, not a pattern.

"Tell me what you think" is Smith's alone, and "Career-limiting" is
Blackburn's alone, from a single episode.

At a meeting on a high pump torque reading, the Marshall Shuttle program
manager, Lindstrom, asked Smith what to do:

> He said, “What’s your opinion?” I said, “Bob, the Science and Engineering position is we should pull the pump.” He said, “I want to know what you think.” I said, “It’s fine. It’s okay.” So we tested, and it was okay. But my boss was very upset with me.

(Smith, p. 23; pre-Challenger; SMI-09)

Blackburn describes a young engineer from Houston who had written a review item
calling for the orbiter's circuit boards to be replaced:

> I said, “This is career-limiting, young man. You put this out there, besides being a laughing stock, you’re going to have some problems.” He refused.

(Blackburn, p. 27; pre-Challenger; BLA-13)

The same theme holds the two counter-cases named above. Blackburn on an argument
with his counterpart Mike, who had flown in from Houston:

> We were having a very elevated, heated discussion on a technical topic. … My secretary came in after he left and she says, “Are you going to get fired?” I said, “I don’t think so.” … I said, “No, we were aggressively discussing issues.”

(Blackburn, p. 20; pre-Challenger; BLA-08, shortened)

Pessin on a technician spraying a primer that turned out to have the wrong
solvent reducer in it:

> The technician sprayed the 1,000-square-foot dome and said, “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.” I think he got a bonus for reporting it, hopefully he did.

(Pessin, p. 19; other; PES-03)

For "I'll pass it on", Blackburn describes a briefing
that an engineer on his staff brought to him the day after the Challenger
accident:

> It was a briefing that he had pitched the October before to one of the review boards about the cold temperature seal effects on the solid rocket boosters. Describing exactly the failure that we had. I looked at it and I said, “Thank you, appreciate that. I’ll pass it on, but I’m sure there are other people that have been looking at this and understand what its impact is.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; pre-Challenger; BLA-17)

### Dimension 2: Concerns absorbed or left unowned

#### Theme C: Split ownership of requirements and risk

Ownership of requirements and risk was split between elements (Sheehan most
clearly), and in one case between NASA and a contractor (BLA-01); problems were
passed along. Sub-tier vendor changes (Pessin, White) are a separate kind of
unowned change.

Four details are not in Table 2:
- Sheehan has 6 of the 10 "Not my requirement" rows, and 8 of the 10 are
  pre-Challenger.
- The vendor rows are Pessin's (5) and White's (3).
- Of the "That's their decision" rows, only BLA-01 is between NASA and a
  contractor.
- "One team, not us and them" is Smith's alone.

Sheehan, describing the period when he was seeking a requirement that the
External Tank prevent ice that could strike the orbiter:

> at the time the Orbiter guys, especially the Orbiter TPS guys working with the silica tile TPS with the reaction-cured glass coating on it, they … a “don’t touch me” kind of attitude. Almost as bad as the Tank guys were, “Well, I don’t have a requirement to preclude ice.” So everybody was very, very parochial.

(Sheehan, p. 11; pre-Challenger; SHE-06)

Sheehan on hardware designers and the launch site:

> It was kick the can down the road. … Many, many, many times I remember, “We’ll let the guys at the Cape figure that out.”

(Sheehan, p. 25; pre-Challenger; SHE-12, shortened: the opening fragment that completes a quotation from p. 24 is omitted)

Vendor changes are a separate kind. Pessin, on foam lost from the External Tank's
intertank after a supplier changed a material:

> In this case the vendor made a change—this is again before we started fingerprinting—we didn’t know the change had been made, and he didn’t know what the effects of the change would be.

(Pessin, p. 21; other; PES-05)

White, asked whether suppliers had to disclose such changes:

> No, because some of the stuff they supplied through the system, others didn’t realize that what they were changing was affecting us.

(White, p. 34; other; WHI-12)

Two parts of the data bear against this claim:
- In Sheehan's account, the program eventually recognized the anti-icing
  requirement, after he had briefed it with enough data (SHE-04).
- Smith describes a deliberate effort to build a single NASA–Thiokol team
  (SMI-20, SMI-21).

#### Theme D: Known problems absorbed as routine under pressure

Theme D is reported as two claims: a debris claim (known debris anomalies) and a
pressure claim (schedule and cost pressure).

**Known debris anomalies.** Known debris anomalies were handled as routine:
Pessin, with Smith and Moser s2 on the same point (SMI-19, MOS2-07). The effects
of foam loss on the orbiter had not been analyzed, by Pessin's account (concept
9: PES-06, PES-07 are Pessin's pre-Columbia account; WHI-14 is White on the
Columbia investigation test, where foam holed the wing's reinforced carbon-carbon
and the experts did not expect it; SHE-01 concerns ice debris; the other
concept-9 rows concern other problems).

Of the 7 "We know about foam coming off" rows:
- 5 are Pessin's.
- 5 are pre-Columbia, all Pessin's except SMI-19.
- Two of Pessin's rows (PES-09, PES-10) are secondhand: he had retired by then.

Pessin on how foam loss was treated with Johnson Space Center:

> Really Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and to a degree Johnson, because when we dealt with the Johnson guys foam coming off was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety.

(Pessin, p. 28; pre-Columbia; PES-08)

Pessin, secondhand, on a foam loss two flights before Columbia. The External Tank
project sent its deputy manager to the program's change board to open an
in-flight anomaly:

> The program said, “We don’t need an in-flight anomaly, we know about foam coming off.” The program manager turned to the ET project manager and said, “Do a study to see what you can do to improve it.”

(Pessin, p. 28; pre-Columbia; PES-10)

Pessin on the External Tank engineering:

> But one thing that we, Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, didn’t do was a technique called process deviation analysis. … We, Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and JSC didn’t understand the failure effects of foam coming off.

(Pessin, p. 27; pre-Columbia; PES-06, shortened)

Two rows in the same evidence are attempts to stop the routinizing:
- Moser told a tile engineer that debris impact could not simply be declared
  acceptable, and set out three choices (MOS2-08).
- The External Tank project's deputy tried to open an in-flight anomaly (PES-09).

**Schedule and cost pressure.** Schedule and cost pressure shaped what was tested
and accepted, mostly in pre-Challenger tile, structures and engine work (concept
7).

Of the 12 "Wink-wink, nod-nod" rows, 10 are pre-Challenger:
- tile and structures: Moser, 5 rows;
- engine: Smith, 2 rows;
- orbiter changes: Blackburn, 1 row;
- processing timelines: Sheehan, 2 rows.

The other 2 are from the Challenger return to flight (Smith, Mitchell).

Sheehan on the planned turnaround time for the orbiter between flights:

> We all did “wink-wink,” “nod-nod,” “yep sure,” that’s the timeline. But that’s the timeline that was required to get the mission model to get the launch flight rate to get the cost per pound figures that the Agency was using with the Congress to show how cheap and efficient Shuttle was going to be.

(Sheehan, p. 26; pre-Challenger; SHE-13)

The claim rests partly on speakers who themselves say safety was not
compromised. Moser, on the structural test program cut back for budget:

> Had we had the money that we set the program out with, we wouldn’t have done this, but we did not compromise safety at all.

(Moser, session 1, p. 24; pre-Challenger; MOS-06)

**The two claims are not linked in the data.** The data does not link the debris claim
to the pressure claim. No "We know about foam coming off" quotation mentions schedule, cost or
pressure, and no "Wink-wink, nod-nod" row is about debris.

#### A synthesis across Themes C and D

*Researcher's synthesis, not a coded finding.*

Read together, the ownership claim (Theme C) and the debris claim describe how a
concern could exist and still not be owned or acted on. Three pages code the two
themes side by side:
- **Smith p. 35:** finger pointing over where debris came from (SMI-18), beside
  the External Tank project's rationale that nothing large enough would come off
  (SMI-19).
- **Moser session 2, p. 10:** a push to call debris impact acceptable (MOS2-07),
  beside Moser on who may accept that risk (MOS2-08).
- **Sheehan p. 26:** designers leaving checkout questions to the launch site
  (SHE-14), beside a turnaround timeline he knew would not be met (SHE-13). This
  pairs Theme C with the pressure claim, not the debris claim.

In a counter-case, Sheehan's anti-icing concern was passed between elements and
was eventually taken up as a program requirement after briefings (SHE-04).

### Dimension 3: What the accidents added to the work

Dimension 3 has one theme: Theme E, "What the accidents added: more checking,
separate oversight, licence to ask why". The theme has no pre-Challenger or pre-Columbia rows. Its rows by era:
- Challenger return to flight: 11 rows (Smith 4, Pessin 3, Mitchell 2, Blackburn
  1, White 1).
- Columbia return to flight: 8 rows, all Singer's.
- Other: 1 row (White).

After Challenger, practice added checking, separate quality/safety
organization, and paperwork ("Go back and review everything"; "An independent
voice that could holler stop"). After Columbia, one informant, Singer, reports a
higher proof standard and licence to ask why ("I believe you, but demonstrate
it").

The separate-organization point rests on:
- Mitchell's account of the Rogers Commission requirement (MIT-01, MIT-03);
- Smith's objection to how Quality's independence worked (SMI-22);
- Pessin on an outside-led review (PES-18).

By concept:
- **"Go back and review everything":** 7 rows are from the Challenger return to
  flight, 1 from the Columbia return to flight (Singer) and 1 is undated (White).
- **"An independent voice that could holler stop":** all rows are from the
  Challenger return to flight.
- **"I believe you, but demonstrate it":** all rows (Singer's) are from the
  Columbia return to flight.

Blackburn on the return to flight after Challenger:

> The return to flight management’s reaction to Challenger was every single requirement and thing that we have done is suspect. “You will go back and review everything you did.”

(Blackburn, p. 29; Challenger return to flight; BLA-16)

Smith on the design reviews for the redesigned solid rocket motor, in which
reviewers wrote up review item discrepancies (RIDs):

> Needless to say, the engineering community post-Challenger was very risk-averse. If it was something that they had any responsibility for, they would write it up. As a consequence there were thousands of RIDs generated in these reviews.

(Smith, p. 33; Challenger return to flight; SMI-16)

Smith on the separate Safety and Mission Assurance organization:

> The big push then was the independence of the Quality people from the project, which I had a problem with. Not the independence, but I had Quality people sitting down in another building critiquing what we’re doing, and all I got was notes, “This is a problem; this is a problem.”

(Smith, p. 37; Challenger return to flight; SMI-22, shortened)

Singer, asked whether attitudes toward safety changed after Columbia:

> Before there may have been more of an acceptance that an element had done their homework and it was safe to fly. After Columbia, there was more effort to say, “I believe you, but demonstrate it.”

(Singer, p. 15; Columbia return to flight; SIN-12)

The data also holds additions that were resisted or reversed, and checking that
thinned out. White on the repair paperwork added after Challenger:

> Basically they wanted a lot more, and it took us a long time to convince them that they didn’t need that. We eventually convinced them, “Look. We’re doing thousands of repairs. What are you doing with all this data?” And they admitted they weren’t doing anything, so we convinced them to let us go undocumented.

(White, p. 49; other; WHI-18)

The other two cases are:
- **Smith's objection** (SMI-22, above): critique from Quality arrived as notes
  from another building.
- **An uncoded passage from Blackburn** (U-BLA-29): when he returned after
  Columbia, the per-flight material checks once handled by his staff of about
  five were signed off by one person.

## Contribution

This paper gives a bottom-up account, drawn from eight oral histories, of how Shuttle engineers and managers say technical concerns were raised and settled, and what they say the two accidents added. Its contribution is modest and specific. First, it records, in the participants' own terms, one route a concern took in the development years: the raiser had to prove the case to repeated probing, often by a test, most clearly in the tile and structures work before the first flight. Second, it records places where a concern could lack an owner: between elements, and with sub-tier vendors who changed a material or its process without telling the program. It also records Pessin's account of a debris anomaly handled as routine before Columbia. Third, it records what these informants say the accidents added: more checking, a separate quality organization and more paperwork after Challenger, and, from Singer alone, a higher standard of proof after Columbia. The paper does not explain either launch decision, it does not test any theory, and it makes no claim about NASA in general. I have not checked how Edmondson (1999) measures psychological safety, so I leave open whether this account connects to it.

## Limitations

The sample is eight interviewees, nine transcripts, from NASA's oral history programme: seven interviewees from the STS Recordation Oral History Project, and Moser's two sessions, which carry the Johnson Space Center Oral History Project header. I chose them, and I excluded two: Thomas, on my own reading of his transcript, and Odom, on Claude's page-cited reading of his whole transcript. The page ranges used for coding were chosen by several Claude instances, and I did not check what they missed. Claude applied my 17 concepts and drafted the inclusion rules; there was no second human coder and no test of agreement. I reviewed weak fits and set aside 34, but another reader might set aside others. Four concepts rest on one interviewee (1, 2, 13, 17), and the Columbia half of Dimension 3 is Singer alone. Only 8 of 121 rows fall between the 1988 return to flight and Columbia, so the paper says little about how practice changed in those years. Dimension 1's strongest support is the pre-Challenger tile and structures work, which is the part of it I describe most firmly, and most of Dimension 2's debris account is Pessin's, partly secondhand. The interviews were given in 2010 and 2011, after both accidents, and the transcripts are edited, so what the informants say may reflect hindsight and editing. I have not yet checked my procedure against what Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013) require, and I have not checked what Vaughan or Edmondson argue beyond the abstract of Edmondson (1999).
